items.body:
> Design only. Nothing was changed or committed. Repo citations are against `main` @ `95212cad`. Gateway citations carry a `gw:` prefix and are upstream **`docker/mcp-gateway@a34df45d`** (release v0.44.1, read under `~/Code/mcp-gateway`). Brief entries applied: SD-1, SD-5, SD-6, SD-7, SD-10 to SD-17. Related: #414 (memory), #403 (Neo4j read-only), #206 (`general`), #107 / #109 (credential patterns), #241 (SSRF), #392 (gateway auth). ### Summary - **The gateway cannot compartmentalise users, and patching it would be a fork.** - It ignores the inbound request: one `mcp.Server` serves every connection, and nothing reads the HTTP headers it is handed. - Secrets, OAuth tokens, volumes and policy are all per server, never per user. - Its only per-client unit is the MCP *session*. The app's pool shares 4 of those across every user. - The 47 commits since `8f422b60`, including the four hardening commits, change none of this (§A.6). - **The app already has the right shape for tenant-scoped tools.** - The Microsoft Graph tools run in-process. - They take the user from a server-side scope at call time, and they refuse when no user is in scope. - Their credential is attached in one function and never reaches the model. - Every result still goes through the injection guard's chokepoint. - **Recommendation: route C, the hybrid.** The gateway keeps the tenant-neutral servers (`fetch`, `web_search`, `context7`). The tenant-scoped ones move to the in-process path: - memory, per #414 (c2); - Atlassian, on each user's own OAuth; - optionally the two Neo4j read tools. The "internal MCP server" starts as that in-process transport. It becomes a separate process only when a second MCP client needs the same tools. - **Found on the way, and verified by running it:** the current gateway release will not run our stack. - It refuses our `--catalog` path at start-up. - Once that is fixed, it answers the app's unauthenticated connection with `401`. - The compose file does not pin the gateway image, so the next fresh host pulls this release (§F1). **The first slice is small:** pin the gateway image, then turn the classification below into test pins. Neither changes runtime behaviour (§Plan). ### Decisions for the owner 1. **Route.** Adopt C, the hybrid (recommended), and do not patch or fork the gateway? 2. **What "internal MCP server" means.** Should it start as the in-process app-tool transport, which already exists, and become a separate MCP server only when a second client needs the tools? Confirm that this meets your intent (§B.2). 3. **Neo4j.** - Should the two read tools move in-process, over the driver the app already has? Then `neo4j-cypher` leaves the gateway, and the gateway holds no credential and can leave the data network (§C). - Or should they stay on the gateway, read-only per #403? - Either way, confirm that Neo4j stays one graph shared by the whole org, with no per-user content in v1. Per-user content would go to Postgres (§B.4). 4. **`general` and the guard.** - `general` already receives the nine `graph_*` tools with no injection guard. It would receive every new tenant-scoped tool the same way. - Either answer #206 D1 and guard `general` before any new connector lands (recommended), or filter tenant-scoped namespaces out of its `tools.all` until then. - Your 2026-09-28 direction for `general` needs Graph, so the filter would work against it (§B.6). 5. **Re-promote #109 (Pattern B)?** That means a per-user connection broker, with Atlassian on its own 3LO OAuth as the first provider. It would be built generically, so the next provider is one module rather than a new design (§B.5). 6. **Sequencing with #414.** Does #414 (a), removal, land first, and is (c2) Phase 3 here? 7. **Background runs (SD-16).** May tenant-scoped tools run under action tokens? Each per-user connector widens what a leaked action token buys, until the planned token table and runner gate land. 8. **Keys and rows (SD-17).** - Set a dedicated `TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, escrowed separately, before a second provider's refresh tokens are stored? - Should new per-user tables bind `user_id` (and the provider) into the AES-GCM envelope as additional data, so that one user's row cannot be swapped into another's? Neither envelope does that today (§S.4). 9. **The gateway upgrade (§F1).** Pin the image by digest now, and land #392 step 1 plus the catalog-path move before any host runs v0.43.1 or later? Should that be split into its own issue? 10. **The dev-only tenant-scoped servers** are `redis`, `database-server`, `rust-mcp-filesystem` and `playwright`. Keep them in the laptop default (`--enable-all-servers`)? Or remove them from the base compose file, so that a shared dev environment cannot inherit them by accident (§1)?
1. Server classification **Rule.** A server is **tenant-neutral** only when neither its credential nor its data differs per user. A server whose data is shared on purpose is **org-shared**: acceptable on a shared credential only while it is read-only, and only while every allow-listed user is entitled to everything in it. Anything else is **tenant-scoped**. "Preview" means the allow-list at `docker-compose.prod.yaml:95`. Dev is `--enable-all-servers` (`docker-compose.yaml:72`), which starts every catalog entry (`docker-compose.prod.yaml:81-87`). | Server | Where | Credential | Class | Reason | |---|---|---|---|---| | `fetch` | dev + preview | none (`configs/custom-catalog.yaml:29-35`) | **neutral** (data) | Public web content. **Network caveat:** the gateway attaches every spawned server to its own networks (`gw:pkg/gateway/clientpool.go:357-364`, `gw:pkg/gateway/network.go:9-29`). In compose that is `app-network` (`docker-compose.yaml:87-88`), so this container shares a network with Postgres, Redis, Neo4j and the app. That is the #241 class (§S.3). | | `web_search` | dev + preview | none (`custom-catalog.yaml:37-43`) | **neutral** | Public search. The declared `allowHosts` (`:42-43`) is enforced only under `--block-network` (`gw:clientpool.go:535`), which neither compose file passes. | | `context7` | dev + preview | none configured (`custom-catalog.yaml:45-55`) | **neutral** | Public library docs. | | `neo4j-cypher` | dev + preview | one Neo4j login, the same superuser the app uses (`custom-catalog.yaml:13-27`, `configs/mcp-config.yaml:14-20`, `docker-compose.prod.yaml:132-133`) | **org-shared**, writable today | The welcome page discloses "one shared graph, the same one for everybody" (`docs/PREVIEW-WELCOME.md:33-36`). The config still ships `read_only: false` (`mcp-config.yaml:20`; #403). Cypher written by the model cannot be scoped to an owner (§B.4), and APOC gives it outbound HTTP (#241). | | `memory` | dev + preview | none | **tenant-scoped** (data) | One volume for the whole host (`custom-catalog.yaml:103-104`); #414. | | `redis` | dev only | empty password (`mcp-config.yaml:41-47`) | **tenant-scoped** (data) | It is the app's own Redis. The Data Stash in it is keyed by session, not owner (`docker-compose.prod.yaml:73-76`; SD-11). | | `database-server` | dev only | Postgres superuser on the app's own database (`mcp-config.yaml:49-51`) | **tenant-scoped**, the worst | Arbitrary SQL over every user's rows, including the encrypted token store (`docker-compose.prod.yaml:76-77`). `connect_to_database` (`custom-catalog.yaml:170`) also takes a database URL the model chooses. | | `rust-mcp-filesystem` | dev only | none | **tenant-scoped** (data) | One writable directory for everyone (`mcp-config.yaml:31-36`). | | `playwright` | dev only | none | **tenant-scoped** (state) | `longLived: true` (`custom-catalog.yaml:188`) keeps one browser per gateway session, and its cookies and storage outlive the call. It also offers `browser_evaluate` / `browser_run_code`, and it sits on the same network as `fetch`. | | gateway dynamic tools (`mcp-add`, `mcp-config-set`, …) | dev only | n/a | **tenant-scoped** (state) | They mutate the shared gateway configuration for every session (`gw:pkg/gateway/configset.go:146`, `gw:pkg/gateway/mcpadd.go:82-85`; the SDK notifies all sessions). They are off whenever `--servers` is set. | | `atlassian` (in `configs/catalog.yaml`, which is not loaded) | — | one API token or PAT per server (`configs/catalog.yaml:1504`, secrets `:1559-1570`) | **tenant-scoped** (credential) | Every user would act as the token's owner in Jira and Confluence. | | in-app `graph_*` (9 tools) | dev + preview | each user's delegated Entra token | **tenant-scoped, done right** | The reference model for route B (§B.1). | **Dev stays safe only while "dev" means one person's laptop.** ADR-0007's shared dev VM is meant to run the production overlay (`docs/PREVIEW.md` §12: each environment is "a complete copy of §§3–7"). Nothing yet pins that it does (decision 10).
A. Route A: make the gateway user-addressable **A.1 Can a request carry a user identity that reaches a server? No.** - **One server for every request.** The streamable-HTTP handler ignores the request and returns one shared server: `NewStreamableHTTPHandler(func(_ *http.Request) *mcp.Server { return g.mcpServer }, nil)` (`gw:pkg/gateway/transport.go:59-61`). - **Headers arrive and are never read.** The Go SDK attaches the inbound headers to each request (`RequestExtra{… Header: req.Header}`, `gw:vendor/github.com/modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk/mcp/streamable.go:1146`, field at `shared.go:481`). Gateway code only passes `Extra` along; it never reads it (the lane's grep of `pkg/` and `cmd/`). - **Gateway auth is one shared bearer token.** It is compared in constant time against a single value (`gw:pkg/gateway/auth.go:53-87`), taken from `MCP_GATEWAY_AUTH_TOKEN` or generated. It authenticates a client to the gateway, never a user to a server. - **Remote servers** get only catalog headers plus that server's own secrets (`gw:pkg/mcp/remote.go:88-92`). - **Container servers** get only the server's own config and secrets (`gw:clientpool.go:352-454`). - **Policy has no caller.** `policy.Request` carries catalog, profile, server, tool and action (`gw:pkg/policy/policy.go:43-60`). The audit record names only the MCP client's name and version (`gw:pkg/gateway/policy_audit.go:41-55`). **A.2 Can it run separate instances per user? Per session, yes. Per user, no.** - **The pool is keyed by session.** It uses `clientKey{serverName, session *mcp.ServerSession}` (`gw:clientpool.go:22-25`). A long-lived or remote server is cached under that key (`:71-84`, `:95-121`) and released when the session closes (`gw:pkg/gateway/run.go:298-305`). - **A server that is not long-lived** gets one container per tool call (`gw:clientpool.go:122-124,143-158`). - **So one MCP session per user would give each user their own processes** (the app's pool is 4 shared connections today, `packages/harness-patterns/mcp-client.server.ts:27-30,77-91`). That is **not tenancy.** - The processes would mount the same static volume (`custom-catalog.yaml:103-104`). - They would carry the same per-server secrets (`gw:pkg/gateway/configuration.go:95-102`). - They would see the same tool list. - It would also make the MCP session an authentication token, which the MCP spec forbids: "MCP Servers **MUST NOT** use sessions for authentication" ([security best practices, Session Hijacking](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/security_best_practices)). - **Secrets are resolved when configuration is read,** never per call: at boot, on reload, on `mcp-add` and on profile activation (`gw:run.go:238,410-436`; `gw:mcpadd.go:92-96`). - **The one seam that looks like namespacing is disabled.** Profile secret namespacing is commented out: `// TODO: Namespace prefix disabled for testing` (`gw:pkg/gateway/configuration_workingset.go:88-91,135-140`). The docs say "Secrets are scoped across all servers rather than for each profile" (`gw:docs/profiles.md:400`). - **OAuth tokens for remote servers are stored per server or provider:** - Desktop and community modes use the key `docker/mcp/oauth/`. - CE mode keys on the authorisation endpoint plus the provider (`gw:pkg/oauth/token_store.go:16-22`). - Refresh runs per server name (`gw:run.go:68`). - **Profiles are chosen when the gateway starts** (`--profile`, `gw:run.go:101-102`). Runtime activation merges into the shared configuration (`gw:pkg/gateway/activateprofile.go:173-205`). **A.3 How big is a patch, and is it upstreamable?** - **The minimal patch.** These sizes are the research lane's inference, not measured: - Read a signed identity header in `handlers.go`, about 30-60 lines. - Key the pool by (user, server) and fix release and invalidation, about 80-150 lines (`gw:clientpool.go`, `gw:run.go`). - Resolve per-user secrets at spawn, about 100-200 lines across `clientpool.go`, `configuration.go`, `secrets_uri.go`, `remote.go` and the OAuth stores. - Reap idle per-user containers, which does not exist today: about 60-100 lines. - Tests on top of all four. - **Three things the patch would still not cover:** - **A per-user secret source.** Nothing per-user exists; the gateway would have to call back into the app. - **Per-user volume names.** The `{{…}}` templates are evaluated against server config, not identity (`gw:clientpool.go:397-430`). - **Per-user tool lists.** Those need one `mcp.Server` per user (`gw:transport.go:59-61`), which is a much larger change. - **Upstream would probably not take it.** - The docs state no multi-user stance at all. The trust model is one local OS user (`gw:docs/security.md:14-19`). OAuth is designed around "secret storage … on the user's machine" (`gw:docs/oauth-flows.md:139`). - A per-user identity header is a new trust model, not a feature inside the current one. - There is no CLA or DCO, and `CODEOWNERS` is `@docker/ai-tools-team`. Acceptance is unknown, so **plan for a fork.** - **The fork would track a fast-moving upstream.** It moved 47 commits between 2026-06-25 and 2026-09-16, and several rewrote exactly the files the patch touches (`clientpool.go`, `handlers.go`, `oauth/*`). Today we run the upstream image unpinned (`docker-compose.yaml:69`), so a fork also means building and pinning our own image. **A.4 What does a container per user per server cost?** - **Measured idle RSS** of four catalog images on the dev laptop (arm64, `docker top`, started and idle, no MCP session): - `memory` 51 MB - `fetch` 64 MB - `context7` 64 MB - `neo4j-cypher` 109 MB - **Cold start, measured.** A cold container answered `initialize` + `tools/list` in 0.15-0.6 s with the image already pulled. - **The gateway's cap is generous.** It applies `--cpus 1 --memory 2Gb` to each container by default (`gw:cmd/docker-mcp/commands/gateway.go:36-41`, applied at `gw:clientpool.go:328-333`). That is a cap, not a reservation. - **The arithmetic, which is inference.** - Long-lived instances of the two tenant-scoped servers we would actually run per user (`memory` + `neo4j-cypher`, about 160 MB) cost about 1.6 GB for 10 active users and about 4.8 GB for 30. - Atlassian through the gateway would add a Python server of the same class (not measured). - On an 8 GB VM that also hosts Neo4j, redis-stack, Postgres, Node and the sandboxes, that does not fit. The tracked sizing already calls 16 GiB "not generous" for one stack (`docs/PREVIEW.md:48,56`), and the overlay records that nobody has measured the box (`docker-compose.prod.yaml:32`). - Per-call containers avoid the idle cost but keep none of the server's state between calls, and `memory` would still mount the one shared volume. **A.5 The no-patch variant: one gateway per user.** #414 (b) already costed this: - N processes, each mounting the Docker socket (`docker-compose.yaml:80`, root-equivalent); - per-user routing in the app; - lifecycle work as people join and leave; - cost linear in users. It still inherits A.2's per-server credentials. **A.6 The four commits the coordinator named, and the rest of the range.** None of them adds per-session or per-user state. The session-keyed pool predates the range. - **`5efe498e` "Preserve session and registry boundaries."** - Code-mode calls now carry the calling request's session (`gw:pkg/codemode/exec.go:81-87`). - `mcp-add` and `mcp-config-set` on a server that is not already enabled now need an enforcing policy provider (`gw:configset.go:174-181`). An already-enabled server can still be reconfigured with no enforcing policy, because the no-op client allows everything (`gw:pkg/policy/policy.go:85-87`). - **`7d332bd6` "Complete policy telemetry and profile authorization."** Profile activation goes through the same management check (`gw:activateprofile.go:134`), and telemetry moved outside the policy gate (`gw:pkg/gateway/tool_policy.go:62-107`). - **`35c3c1d7` "Harden OAuth and tool policy boundaries."** - The CE token keys became collision-resistant, but they are still keyed per provider (`gw:token_store.go:16-64`). - It adds revocation. - Remote requests and redirects must stay on the same origin (`gw:remote.go:232-264`). - **`3640bafe` "Harden OAuth discovery and tool dispatch."** It adds one invoke-policy gate for direct calls, `mcp-exec` and code-mode (`gw:tool_policy.go:18-57`), and hardens discovery validation. - **The rest of the range is OAuth, secrets-engine and allowlist-casing work.** Two commits do affect us, but in a different way (§F1): `42e1359a`, which requires auth in container mode, and `9aad4a57`, which constrains local catalog paths.
B. Route B: a hames-owned path for tenant-scoped tools **B.1 What already exists: the Graph connector is route B, shipped.** - **Identity is ambient and server-side.** `runWithRequestContext({ userId, sessionId }, …)` opens an AsyncLocalStorage scope (`app/src/lib/harness-client/request-user.server.ts:33-58`). The one turn implementation opens it for interactive, triggered and approval runs alike (`app/src/lib/harness-client/turn.server.ts:13-23,252`), after the caller has authenticated (`app/src/lib/auth/server.ts:16-28`; `turn.server.ts:33-36` explains why that module is deliberately not `'use server'`). - **The registry reads the user at call time and refuses without one** (`packages/connectors/app-tools/registry.ts:144-175`). Its stated invariants: no credential field in any advertised schema, and executors resolve their own tokens (`:23-31`). A pin enforces the schema half for every registered app tool (`packages/connectors/__tests__/graph/graph-connectors.test.ts:27-38`). - **The credential is attached in one place.** `graphFetch` loads the user's encrypted MSAL cache, acquires a token silently and writes the rotated cache back (`app/src/lib/auth/graph-token.server.ts:67-129`). It then sets `Authorization` with `Headers.set`, so no caller can override it (`:220-237`). The token is never returned to tool code (`:163-194`). - **The store** is keyed by `user_id` (`app/src/lib/auth/user-tokens.server.ts:34-43`) and AES-256-GCM encrypted (`app/src/lib/auth/secret-crypto.server.ts:34-94`). Cross-user interleaving is pinned (`app/src/__tests__/lib/app-tools/token-isolation.test.ts`). - **It is a process transport,** consulted after the run's scoped transports and before the gateway (`app/src/lib/app-tools/index.server.ts:97-110`; `packages/harness-patterns/mcp-client.server.ts:373-379`; the order is pinned by `transport-precedence.test.ts`). - **Precedent for per-call identity.** The sandbox's tenant is a *function* evaluated per run, never a string captured at build time: "a tenant that arrived as input is not an isolation boundary, it is a parameter" (`app/src/lib/harness-client/session.server.ts:78-100`). The same rule applies to every tool here, because patterns are cached per session (`:118-122,175-180`). **B.2 In-process or a separate internal MCP server.** | | B1: in-process (the app-tool transport) | B2: separate internal MCP server | |---|---|---| | How identity arrives | the ALS value; no token crosses any boundary | the app mints a short-lived JWT per request (`sub` = user, `aud` = the internal server, `exp` ≤ 60 s, `jti`). It travels as `Authorization` through the SDK transport's `fetch` hook (`fetch?: FetchLike`, SDK 1.29.0 `client/streamableHttp.d.ts:81`), which runs inside the caller's ALS scope, so the pooled connection does not pin one identity. The server verifies it on every request. | | What it costs | nothing new: the seam, the guard path and the tests exist | a second process, a fourth key to escrow (SD-17), its own network posture, a new test layer, and a way to keep the session from becoming the authentication (A.2) | | When it is worth it | now | when a second MCP client (an IDE, Claude Desktop) must reach the same per-user tools, or when credential custody has to leave the app process | The MCP spec forbids passing the user's upstream token through to either path: "MCP servers **MUST NOT** accept any tokens that were not explicitly issued for the MCP server" ([Token Passthrough](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/security_best_practices)). **Recommendation: B1 now.** `AppToolDefinition` is already MCP-shaped (name, description, input schema, execute; `registry.ts:50-58`), so moving to B2 later is mechanical. One optional tidy-up. The request identity is a second ALS, opened on the same line as the run frame (`turn.server.ts:252-253`). #374 merged five stores into the frame because "five openers means five chances to skip one" (`packages/harness-patterns/run-frame.server.ts:6-15`). An opaque `principal` slot would fold identity in. Tenancy does not depend on it. **B.3 Where tenancy is enforced, per tool.** There are two different questions, and each tool family answers them in one place. | Tool family | Whose authority? enforced by | Whose data? enforced by | |---|---|---| | `graph_*` (exists) | Entra, through the user's delegated token | Entra | | `atlassian_*` (proposed) | Atlassian, through the user's 3LO token with read-only scopes | Atlassian | | `memory_*` (proposed, #414 c2) | n/a | our repository module: `WHERE user_id = $1` on every statement. An id the model names, such as `memory_id`, is always matched together with `AND user_id = $1`. | | Neo4j org graph | one shared login (org-shared) | nobody, by design. It must hold only content every user may read. | Two rules hold for all of them: - No schema field names a user, owner, tenant, session or token. - A call that cannot get the user's credential ends as "connect your account". It never falls back to a shared credential. **B.4 Neo4j on Community Edition.** - **What Community lacks.** Multiple databases and role-based access control are Enterprise-only ([Neo4j edition comparison](https://neo4j.com/docs/operations-manual/current/introduction/)). The running container reports `NEO4J_EDITION=community` (#241 comment). - **Why model-written Cypher cannot be scoped.** - A READ transaction bounds writes and nothing else (`packages/connectors/neo4j/queries.ts:68-70`; #241). A model-written `MATCH (n)` reads every node in the database whatever predicate we hoped it would carry. - Rewriting the query text to add one is the textual barrier SD-14 rules out. - **So tenancy in Neo4j is only possible where the model does not write the Cypher.** - **The design:** 1. **The shared org graph keeps model-written read Cypher.** It is read-only per #403, uses the procedure allow-list from #241, and holds nothing a colleague may not read. 2. **Per-user graph content does not live in that database in v1.** It goes to Postgres, as #414 (c2) does for memory. 3. **If per-user graph data is wanted later, use intent-shaped tools whose Cypher we own.** Today's edit ops are the model for that: they own their Cypher, validate identifiers and take only parameters (`packages/connectors/neo4j/graph-edit.server.ts:9-17,75-127`). - Each would carry an `owner: $userId` predicate on every `MATCH` and `CREATE`, with `$userId` taken from the ALS. - They would run against a database the model-written Cypher cannot reach: either a second Neo4j container (the image is about 840 MB, and the JVM heap is not measured) or a multi-database fork such as DozerDB (unvetted). - Today's edit ops are identity-free (`graph-edit.server.ts:1-17`), which is correct only while the graph is disclosed as shared. **B.5 Memory and Atlassian on this seam.** - **Memory (#414 c2).** A Postgres table: - `user_id` stays plaintext for scoping; the content is under `DATA_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (`app/src/lib/db/crypto.server.ts:183-216`, fail-closed); - it is stamped with the inference tier it was written under (SD-12); - three tools in the registry; - erasure is `DELETE … WHERE user_id = $1`. - Recalled text was often written during a turn that read untrusted content, so the consuming agent guards the `memory` namespace (stored injection, SD-1). - **Atlassian. The stopped lane's option O5, re-checked against the repo:** - Each user connects their own account with OAuth 2.0 3LO, read-only scopes plus `offline_access`. - Refresh tokens rotate and expire after 90 days of inactivity. - Atlassian's rules forbid collecting API tokens or asking each customer to create their own 3LO app ([Atlassian 3LO docs](https://developer.atlassian.com/cloud/jira/platform/oauth-2-3lo-apps/)). - A generic `user_connections (user_id, provider)` table holds the encrypted token sets. - `providerFetch(userId, provider, path)` mirrors `graphFetch`: the credential is attached in one place and the host is allow-listed (§S.3). - Five read tools, in which the server composes JQL and CQL. That mirrors the Graph KQL precedent (`packages/connectors/graph/graph-tools.server.ts:35-37`). - A dedicated agent guarded with `namespaces: ['atlassian']`. - The lane's runner-up is a per-user MCP client to Atlassian's Rovo server (O3). That is B2's shape pointed at a vendor. Its Rovo-specific facts were not re-verified here. - The lane's provider-specific decisions belong to the build issue: site pinning, scope set, tenant-admin checks. - **Size reference, inference only:** the Graph connector is 9 tools in 1,921 lines (`graph-tools.server.ts`), plus a 364-line token module. An Atlassian v1 with five read tools is smaller. Most of the cost is the OAuth broker, built once for every provider. **B.6 The injection guard still applies, and `general` is the gap.** - **The chokepoint covers in-process tools.** It wraps dispatch, above scoped transports, process transports and the gateway (`mcp-client.server.ts:326-353`; SD-6; `injection-guard-chokepoint.test.ts`). A tenant-scoped tool is therefore sanitised as long as the consuming agent declares its namespace. - **The namespace must be one the catalog produces** (`packages/harness-patterns/patterns/withInjectionGuard.server.ts:277-311`; SD-5). The transport's `namespaceFor` is consulted first (`packages/harness-patterns/tools.server.ts:153-158`), so declaring `namespace: 'atlassian'` on the tool is enough. - **The precedent:** `microsoft-365` guards `graph` because "the per-user Graph token authenticates WHO fetched a document, not WHO WROTE it" (`packages/agents/agents/microsoft-365.server.ts:115-123`). The same holds for Jira comments and Confluence pages. - **The gap.** `listTools()` appends every process transport's tools to the gateway's (`mcp-client.server.ts:499-511`). `general` hands `tools.all` to its planner and its loop with no guard (`packages/agents/agents/general.server.ts:57,63`; SD-7, #206). - So the nine `graph_*` tools already run unguarded, in the same loop as `fetch`. - Every connector added here would join them (decision 4). - **Tenancy does not stop exfiltration.** Tenancy bounds *whose* data a turn can reach, not where that data can be sent. A loop holding one user's mail and `fetch` can still be steered into sending that user's own mail out. That is the guard's job (SD-1), not this design's.
C. Route C: the hybrid, and what it costs **The shape:** | Plane | Servers | Credential | Isolation | |---|---|---|---| | Gateway | `fetch`, `web_search`, `context7` | none | not needed | | In-process | `graph_*` (exists), `memory_*`, `atlassian_*`, and optionally `read_neo4j_cypher` / `get_neo4j_schema` | each user's own credential, or org-shared and read-only | §B.3 | | Removed from shared hosts | `memory` (#414), `redis`, `database-server`, `rust-mcp-filesystem`, `playwright` | — | — | **Moving Neo4j in-process (decision 3) pays for itself.** - The app already has a READ-mode session and a model-text query path (`packages/connectors/neo4j/queries.ts:68-70,272-316`). - Once Neo4j moves, the gateway holds no credential at all, which is #108's own note: "if routed via the pooled neo4j-driver, the gateway stops holding this secret at all". - The gateway no longer needs `app-network`, so `fetch` can be moved onto a network that reaches the internet and nothing internal (§S.3). Today the gateway joins `app-network` (`docker-compose.yaml:87-88`) and hands that network to every server it spawns. **What the hybrid costs:** 1. **Two planes with different rules.** Someone adding a server has to classify it first. §1's rule becomes a test pin (Phase 1), so that a tenant-scoped server on the allow-list fails CI rather than review. 2. **Connector code we own** instead of catalog config: an OAuth broker, a token store and the tool bodies (§B.5 sizes). That is the price of per-user authority, and no route avoids it. Route A only moves it into Go and into a fork. 3. **The gateway remains** a Docker-socket holder (`docker-compose.yaml:80`) serving three public tools, and it still has to be kept working (§F1). 4. **Neo4j moving in-process keeps model-written Cypher.** #241's procedure allow-list and an egress policy are still needed, wherever that code runs. 5. **Every connector widens the action-token front door** until the planned hardening lands (SD-16, decision 7).

Identity is a header the gateway must trust. Secrets, volumes and tool lists stay per server unless they are also patched. | Weak. Separate processes, but the same credential and the same volume (A.2) | **Strong.** The ALS identity is read per call. The provider enforces authority; the repository enforces data. | Strong, if every request carries an app-minted, audience-scoped token | **Strong** for scoped tools; neutral tools need none | | **Effort** | L: ~270-510 lines of Go (inference) in 6+ files, plus a per-user secret source that does not exist, plus app-side signing | M: per-user routing and pools in the app | M per connector; the seam exists | L: B1 plus a server, auth and deployment | **M**: B1 plus config | | **Maintenance** | High: a fork of a repo that moved 47 commits in 12 weeks, in these files | Medium: lifecycle per user | Low to medium: our code, in our test pyramid | Medium to high | **Low to medium** | | **Resource cost** | ~50-110 MB idle per user per server (measured). ~4.8 GB at 30 users for two servers (inference) | the same, plus a gateway per user | ~0 extra | +1 process | **~0 extra**; removing `memory` saves a container | | **Security** | Larger Docker-socket blast radius; trust rests on a header; OAuth custody stays in the gateway's credential store | N processes holding the Docker socket | Credentials stay in the process that already holds them; the guard chokepoint covers it | One more hop and one more key to protect | The gateway can become credential-free and leave the data network | | **Fit with the €50 one-VM plan** | Poor | Poor | **Good** | Fair | **Good** | **About the €50 one-VM figure.** It comes from the dispatch. I found no tracked document for it. The tracked records size one stack at `Standard_D4s_v5`, 4 vCPU / 16 GiB (`docs/PREVIEW.md:48`), and ADR-0007 plans two VMs. The resource row is judged against an 8 GB box.
S. Security **S.1 Identity propagation and token handling** - **In-process (B1).** No token crosses a boundary: the identity is the ALS value set from the authenticated session. - Provider access tokens are short-lived and audience-scoped by the provider: Graph's for Graph, Atlassian's for `api.atlassian.com`. - They are acquired per call and attached in one function (`graph-token.server.ts:220-237`). - Refresh tokens exist only encrypted at rest. - **Out of process (B2).** An app-minted JWT per request (§B.2). Never the user's Entra token, and never the MCP session. - **Never in the model's context.** - The schema pin (`graph-connectors.test.ts:27-38`). - Errors that carry no stack or credential (`registry.ts:168-173`). - Auth failures that do not echo the provider's body (`graph-token.server.ts:184-191`). - The pin's word list should grow to include `owner`, `tenant` and `session` (Phase 1). **S.2 The `'use server'` gate (SD-13)** - **The new browser-reachable surface:** connect, disconnect and list connections; memory list and delete. - **Each module gates first and duplicates its gate** (`app/src/lib/harness-client/actions.server.ts:47-53` is the shape). None takes an owner argument. - **Each joins a source-scan pin like the one for `queries.ts`** (SD-13). - **OAuth `start` and `callback` routes** take the user from the session and check signed state (`app/src/routes/api/auth/login.ts:30-52`, `callback.ts:48-60`). They never read a user id from the query. - **The dev bypass** gives every bypassed caller one identity, and therefore one set of connections (SD-15). That is expected, and it is safe only on a laptop. **S.3 SSRF (#241)** - **Spawned servers share the gateway's networks** (`gw:clientpool.go:357-364`, `gw:network.go:9-29`). - **Verified by running v0.44.1:** the gateway started `fetch` with `--network ` (on a plain `docker run` that was `bridge`). - In compose, that network is `app-network`, beside Postgres, Redis, Neo4j's HTTP port, the app and `doc-convert`. - `fetch` declares no `allowHosts`, and `allowHosts` is enforced only under `--block-network` (`gw:clientpool.go:535`). - **Not verified:** whether `mcp-server-fetch` itself refuses private addresses. - `fetch` is on the preview allow-list, so this is the #241 class reachable from any agent that holds `fetch`. Route C's Neo4j move is what lets the gateway leave that network. - **Per-user fetchers must not accept an absolute URL from the model.** `graphFetch` has an absolute-URL branch for `@odata.nextLink` (`graph-token.server.ts:221`). Today's Graph tools build only encoded relative paths (`graph-tools.server.ts:313-315`). A generic `providerFetch` should allow-list its hosts, so that a model-supplied URL can never carry a user's bearer token off-host. Undici strips `Authorization` on cross-origin redirects (`graph-token.server.ts:151-161`), and that property must hold in any new fetcher. - **Model-written Cypher keeps `apoc.load.*` and `LOAD CSV`** wherever it runs (#241). **S.4 Encryption at rest** - **Credentials** use `encryptSecret` under `TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY`. Unset, that key is derived from `AUTH_SESSION_SECRET` (`secret-crypto.server.ts:34-53`). Set it, and escrow it separately (SD-17, decision 8). - **Per-user content** uses `encryptField` under `DATA_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (`crypto.server.ts:18-29,183-216`). Every new table joins `encryption-coverage.test.ts`. Ids, `user_id` and timestamps stay plaintext for scoping. - **Neither envelope binds its row.** `encryptSecret` takes no additional authenticated data (`secret-crypto.server.ts:56-67`). Anyone who can write the database can move one user's ciphertext into another user's row, and it still decrypts. For `user_tokens`, that hands user B user A's Microsoft session. In dev the `database-server` tool gives the model exactly that write. - Binding `table|user_id|provider` as AAD closes this for new tables. - Retrofitting `user_tokens` is a separate item. - **Erasure.** Every new table needs `DELETE … WHERE user_id = $1`. Disconnect means delete plus provider revocation (SD-11).
F. Side findings **F1. The current gateway release does not run our stack. Verified by execution; not reported before.** I ran `docker/mcp-gateway:v0.44.1` (= `a34df45d`) on a loopback port with our catalog and `--servers=fetch`: 1. **The catalog path is refused at start-up.** - With `--catalog=/mcp/custom-catalog.yaml`, exactly as `docker-compose.yaml:75,82` passes it, the gateway exits: `reading catalog: local file path must resolve within Docker MCP catalogs directory`. - The check is `gw:pkg/catalog/catalog.go:26,133-159`, from `9aad4a57` (2026-06-17, in v0.43.1+). - Mounting the file under `/root/.docker/mcp/catalogs/` starts it. 2. **An unauthenticated `initialize` gets `HTTP 401`.** That is what the app sends: no `Authorization` header at all (`mcp-client.server.ts:113`; #392). - Since `42e1359a` (2026-06-17, v0.43.1+), container mode no longer disables auth (`gw:run.go:493-518`; `gw:transport.go:51-54`). - Neither compose file sets `MCP_GATEWAY_AUTH_TOKEN` or `--allow-unauthenticated` (`docker-compose.yaml:68-93`, `docker-compose.prod.yaml:94-102`). **Why nothing has failed yet.** - `image: docker/mcp-gateway` is unpinned (`docker-compose.yaml:69`). - The laptop's image was built 2026-01-22, before both changes. - The preview runbook's tool-surface check ran on a laptop (`docs/PREVIEW.md:946-961`). - A fresh host, such as ADR-0007's new VMs, pulls a release that has both changes. **The fix:** - pin a digest; - #392 step 1, with the token supplied from `.env`; - move the catalog mount. Neither the deployed VM's image nor the `--config` path was checked. **F2. `mcp-config-set` on an enabled server needs no policy, even after `5efe498e`** (`gw:configset.go:174-181`, `gw:pkg/policy/policy.go:85-87`). With dynamic tools on (dev, `--enable-all-servers`), a model can rewrite an enabled server's config for every session. One example is `neo4j-cypher`'s URI. It is off under `--servers` (the preview). This is decision 10's reason as well.

Write the rule down as pins, with no runtime change.** - **Classification pin.** `app/src/__tests__/lib/preview-tool-surface.test.ts` already pins the allow-list (`:36-39`). It would assert that the allow-list holds only servers §1 classifies as neutral, plus `neo4j-cypher` only while it is read-only. `memory` moves to FORBIDDEN when #414 (a) lands. - **Registry-wide schema pin.** Lift the credential-field scan out of the Graph test into the registry's own tests, and add `owner`, `tenant` and `session`. Then every future connector inherits it. - **Each pin ships with the mutation that turns it red.** - **Size:** one PR, tests only. **Phase 2: the per-user connection broker** (#109, decisions 5, 7 and 8). - The `user_connections` table, with AAD and `TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY`. - Connect, callback and disconnect routes (§S.2). - `providerFetch` with a host allow-list. - Atlassian v1, five read tools, in its own guarded agent. - `general` gets it only after decision 4. **Phase 3: memory as the first data-type tenant tool** (#414 c2, decision 6). **Phase 4: Neo4j in-process** (decision 3). - Reimplement the two read tools over `readSession()`. - Drop `neo4j-cypher` from the gateway. - Move the gateway off `app-network`. - Land #241's procedure allow-list. - Per-user graph content only if it is decided later (§B.4). **Phase 5, only when needed: B2.** Expose the in-process tools as an internal MCP server, with per-request audience-scoped tokens.
Method, and what I did not verify **Verification:** - Repo claims were read at `95212cad`. - Gateway claims were read at `a34df45d`. A research sub-agent mapped them, and I re-read the load-bearing lines. - The stopped Atlassian lane's repo claims were re-checked against source. One was restated more precisely: the per-session cache is the pattern cache (`session.server.ts:118-122`), and `mcp-client.server.ts:494-498` is the comment that describes it. **Measurements**, all throwaway containers removed afterwards: - idle RSS and cold start for four catalog images, run with `--network none`; - the v0.44.1 gateway start-up and its `401`, on a loopback port. **Not verified:** - the preview VM's gateway image and its baseline memory; - whether `mcp-server-fetch` blocks private addresses; - Rovo MCP facts beyond the lane's notes; - the JVM heap of a second Neo4j; - whether `Extra.Header` survives the gateway's interceptor serialization; - every line count marked as inference.

items.title: [UI-015] Specify and qualify a bounded Webflow intelligence execution adapter
items.body:
Parent initiative: https://github.com/weareheadless/crawlseo/issues/3
Project: https://github.com/users/weareheadless/projects/3
Work ID: **UI-015** · Area: Connectors · Phase: Later
Delivery: **Later capability** · Readiness: **Deferred**.

## Reference and requirements

[Reviewed proposal](https://github.com/weareheadless/crawlseo/blob/codex/centralized-intelligence-architecture/docs/architecture/centralized-intelligence/spec.md) · [Delivery plan](https://github.com/weareheadless/crawlseo/blob/codex/centralized-intelligence-architecture/docs/architecture/centralized-intelligence/implementation-plan.md) · [Agent entry](https://github.com/weareheadless/crawlseo/blob/codex/centralized-intelligence-architecture/docs/architecture/centralized-intelligence/agent-workflow.md)
Requirements: **EXEC-007, API-001–002, ACCEPT-003**. Architecture PR: https://github.com/weareheadless/crawlseo/pull/27.
This is design v0.2, not an implemented API. Pin the concrete reviewed contract commit before dependent implementation. Read only relevant requirements and direct prerequisites first.

## Problem and bounded result

Start with supported official Webflow API/source capabilities and an identified adapter owner/repository. Map CMS staged/live state, publication scope, review destinations, receipts and rollback limits. Implement only the agreed bounded pilot; discovery completion does not advertise Webflow execution support. Webflow does not technically depend on Wix implementation; keep it explicitly Deferred until the PM selects this platform and an adapter owner/repository exists. Produce capability discovery before any implementation PR.

## Code starting points

- `lib/connectors/types.ts`
- `lib/connectors/service.ts`
- `docs/site-agent-connector-contract.md`

These are existing repository-relative entry points. Check current main/active PRs and reuse implemented pieces before introducing a new module or schema.

## Dependencies

- https://github.com/weareheadless/crawlseo/issues/15

Native blocking links must match this list. A dependency is satisfied by its reviewed artifact and passing contract checks, not merely a closed issue. Deferred is a scheduling decision even after dependencies pass; do not auto-start it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Capability/API/permission matrix and adapter ownership are documented with current primary references.
- [ ] Review identifies actual publication scope and unrelated pending changes; no assumed page-only atomic publish.
- [ ] Exact candidate, approval, retry, generation and readback fixtures pass in the adapter and CrawlSEO.
- [ ] A separately authorized disposable pilot provides visible live verification before binding support is enabled.
- [ ] Unsupported operations stay analysis/manual/blocked; no customer-specific workaround or schema fork.

## Validation and first PR

Shared connector contract fixtures and explicit Webflow pilot plan/results; no live effect before authorization

For substantive implementation, add focused behavioral tests for the changed boundary and run repository-required checks. Check retry/stale input/wrong-project cases where affected. For discovery/docs, validate paths, schema fixtures and links; do not claim runtime tests or a live pilot. Start with one bounded PR against the first unmet acceptance item; preserve this issue for subsequent coherent PRs if needed instead of bundling a repo-wide rewrite.

## Agent handoff and boundaries

Read repository AGENTS/CLAUDE instructions, check direct dependencies and current claims, then record work ID, baseline, consumed contract SHA, reused code, bounded change and tests in the pickup/PR. Use an isolated `codex/ui-015-...` branch. Link consumer/producer PRs when a wire contract changes. Stop at this issue's acceptance boundary; surface new requirements to the PM.

No new service, queue broker, vector database, generic plugin/workflow framework or universal publishing agent. No customer migration, paid provider dispatch, permission expansion or site publication is authorized by this engineering issue. Keep tenant data/secrets out of public issues. Preserve CMS and exact approval/release authority. Merged is not integrated/live Verified; source effects require their own proven review capability.

   - 100% only when planned execution reaches terminal accounting;
   - terminal summary: succeeded / failed / skipped / jobs collected or updated.
9. Preserve #341/#348 invariant for the current PostgreSQL/GCP runtime:
   - a terminal Run shown as latest run must have a corresponding history record;

- Selection Criteria / GUI filter redesign (#489 already TEST_PASS; #515 handles UX);

- PROD enablement.

- ADMIN aggregation contains no personal identifiers/content;
- `STARTED_RUN` proven on stale/insufficient scope;
- second equivalent concurrent request returns `JOINED_EXISTING_RUN`;
- equivalent requests create only one heavy Run;
- bounded scope reaches actual connectors/provider queries;
- unrelated Jobs Families are not searched for a bounded USER Run;
- shared results are reusable by other profiles;
- one `run_id` is traceable end-to-end;
- source progress reports real `X/Y`;
- terminal Run persists coherent status + history + source outcomes;
- failure after partial provider/corpus work still leaves a terminal/diagnostic Run record;
- no provider call on `REUSED_CORPUS` / `BLOCKED_BY_POLICY`;
- DEV acceptance includes a real new Run, not only mocks/unit tests.

## Required evidence

- exact candidate SHA;
- request-scope examples with no PII;
- provider/connector scope evidence;
- concurrent coalescing evidence;
- `STARTED_RUN` + `JOINED_EXISTING_RUN` live DEV evidence;
- run-id/status/history consistency proof;
- source progress X/Y proof;
- regression proof for #489 bounded `/me/jobs`, lazy FIT and isolation.

items.title: Specification: Concurrent accounts and identifiable maintainable Codex builds
items.body:
# #369: Concurrent accounts and identifiable, maintainable Codex builds

State: APPROVED_FOR_IMPLEMENTATION. Owner: ecochran76 / primary coordinator. Coordinating issue: https://github.com/CochranResearchGroup/codex-wake/issues/369. Related workspace recovery: #368. Operator approved the test boundaries and breakdown and explicitly invoked implement-spec/TDD with independent ticket workers. Implementation is not complete.

## Problem Statement

Switching previously authenticated Codex profiles now repeatedly requests login. The cause and first affected release remain unknown. The current launcher can use an official client against a modified shared backend while both show the same upstream version. The operator wants concurrent accounts, common skills/settings/MCP connections, unified history discovery, genuine stock side-by-side operation, and straightforward upgrades without disrupting work or silently dropping modifications.

## Solution

Extend codex-profiles as the account launcher and shared-configuration owner. Keep account authentication and writable runtime state isolated. Add explicit stock/modded build selection, visible actual client/backend/account identity, and supported cross-profile discovery. Normal resume returns to the owning account. Explicit continuation under another account creates a linked successor. Provide automatic update discovery, reproducible staging and explicit activation/rollback, backed by real installed-path tests in a disposable WSL environment.

## User Stories

1. As an operator, I want to log in once per account so ordinary profile switching retains authentication.
2. As an operator, I want A → B → A to select the correct saved account every time.
3. As an operator, I want accounts A and B running simultaneously without either changing the other's credentials.
4. As an operator, I want existing profile names and aliases preserved.
5. As an operator, I want shell and executable launchers to resolve the same configuration.
6. As an operator, I want plain codex to launch the modified build under my selected account.
7. As an operator, I want an explicit stock command that actually uses an official backend.
8. As an operator, I want a persistent account and STOCK/MODDED indicator reflecting the connected backend.
9. As an operator, I want exact upstream/build/patch identities and supported capabilities inspectable.
10. As an operator, I want one shared skills/settings/MCP configuration to maintain.
11. As an operator, I want supported operator-level MCP logins reused regardless of Codex account.
12. As an operator, I want necessary connector/account/channel overrides explicit and inspectable.
13. As an operator, I want to browse conversations from all selected tenant homes without shared writable databases.
14. As an operator, I want ordinary resume to select the conversation's owning account.
15. As an operator, I want compatible stock and modified builds to access the same tenant's conversations.
16. As an operator, I want duplicate activation of the same conversation prevented across channels.
17. As an operator, I want incompatible versions to preserve my history and explain what is unsupported.
18. As an operator, I want explicit continuation with another account to create a linked successor with available history.
19. As an operator, I want original conversation provenance, goals and cumulative accounting preserved across continuation.
20. As an operator, I want automatic notification of upstream releases and visible custom-build lag.
21. As an operator, I want one command to build, qualify and stage a modified upgrade.
22. As an operator, I want an explicit switch and known-good rollback that preserve running work until cutover.
23. As an operator, I want failed builds/tests to leave my active package intact.
24. As an operator, I want realistic isolated upgrade tests without importing production credentials.
25. As an operator, I want disposable caches and inactive payload archives so testing does not consume primary storage indefinitely.
26. As an operator, I want exact account/channel/conversation identity available to later workspace recovery.
27. As an operator, I want genuine authentication expiry distinguished from an account-routing regression.
28. As an operator, I want explicit partial results and uncertain-operation reconciliation rather than silent fallbacks.

## Implementation Decisions

- codex-profiles owns existing profile aliases, selected account home, effective shared configuration and launch management. Native Codex owns actual client/backend identity, capabilities and complete-package runtime behavior. Wake consumes those identities for lifecycle/continuation; it must not introduce a competing account selector.
- Account selection and stock/modded selection are separate dimensions. Plain codex defaults to modified; the explicit stock command selects an official backend. Distinct runtime endpoint/package selection prevents accidental cross-channel connections.
- Preserve one tenant's conversation identity across compatible channels. Resolve writable database concurrency through the native supported ownership boundary; separate sockets alone do not make two database writers safe. Before removing current profile concurrency restrictions, prove account/channel endpoint isolation and safe native store access. If unsupported, report the limitation rather than silently duplicate or migrate sessions.
- Use versioned, inspectable build manifests for upstream base, patch revision, executable identity and capability results. Show actual account/backend identity at connection, reconnect and resume. Launcher labels alone are insufficient; unsupported stock identity features must be stated rather than represented as verified.
- Keep Codex login credentials account-local using existing native credential-store behavior. Do not rotate, copy or overwrite live credentials to simulate successful switching. Retain existing profile configuration edits during migration.
- Share common settings, skills, rules and MCP server definitions through the existing profile configuration owner. Share operator-level MCP authentication only through the connector's supported scope. Per-account exceptions are explicit. Effective configuration is inspectable; unsupported configuration is surfaced. Shared edits reach new launches; live refresh is explicit and does not silently restart peers.
- Cross-tenant session discovery is read-only and version-aware, retaining owning tenant/native namespace provenance. Ordinary resume routes to that owner. Equal directory names, tab names and latest activity do not establish identity.
- Compatible channel switching retains the tenant's conversation and enforces a durable active-conversation fence. Uncertain prior launch or stale ownership is reconciled from native evidence before another launch. Unknown incompatible schemas hold without destructive conversion.
- Explicit continue-with-account creates a separate linked successor using all available supported history; retain source provenance and disclose unsupported/truncated history. Original records remain intact. Resource/goal continuity must use the existing cumulative allocation owner; absent or exhausted authority does not become a fresh allowance. Preparing/resuming context does not imply replay of uncertain pending actions.
- Automatic update discovery does not activate upgrades. Staging verifies official provenance, applies the minimal versioned patches, produces a complete identifiable package, and runs capability acceptance. Patch conflicts, missing capabilities and failing checks preserve the active version.
- Activate a staged build explicitly, handling affected sessions and durable state compatibility. Rollback is qualified against supported database/history schemas; never promise an executable rollback reverses an irreversible data migration. Keep a compatible snapshot/rollback route or hold activation.
- Use an existing disposable WSL fixture, preserving unrelated contents and placing this lab in a dedicated run directory. Isolate test homes, daemon endpoints, temporary credential stores and provider fixtures; production accounts/secrets are not needed for initial tests. A separate user namespace or isolated keyring must prevent the fixture from reading the host's production credential store.
- Stage active payloads on primary storage, separate rebuildable caches from retained packages and evidence, and archive selected inactive loads to a verified HDD target. Record checksums/provenance and verify restoration before deleting staged copies. Logical VHD space is not physical drive capacity. Never move a live VHD or reset unrelated fixtures.
- Expose tenant, namespace, build/channel, logical binding and supported resume capability for HF-19. Implementing complete Byobu restoration remains #368, not an implicit deliverable here.

## Testing Decisions

Proposed highest public boundary: invoke actual account/channel launchers as subprocesses against isolated real native backends and durable tenant homes; inspect connected account identity, package identity, history, effective configuration and effects. Existing profile CLI tests and native scoped-reload/notice/history-recovery tests supply prior art. Prefer those seams over tests mirroring internal helper logic.

For authentication, first obtain a red-capable deterministic A → B → A regression at the actual launch/auth-storage boundary. Compare pinned known-working and affected builds when evidence identifies them. Test credential reload/refresh rotation with synthetic responses and an isolated test keyring. Shell/executable configuration differences are hypotheses, not established root cause. If supported native auth cannot be simulated faithfully, record the missing boundary and preserve the failure; a fabricated successful login is not acceptance.

The WSL product matrix covers two tenants × stock/modded, sequential switching, parallel distinct conversations, duplicate-conversation rejection, restart, reconnect, shared config/MCP resolution, schema compatibility refusal, staged upgrade failure, activation and compatible rollback. Test foreign explicit endpoints and mismatched client/backend identity. Start with owned local fixtures and no external provider calls.

Native capability qualification covers scoped MCP reload without peer disturbance, durable notices without model work, genuine caller/accounting provenance and orphan-output recovery. Unsupported stock capabilities are expected explicit differences. Identify source, package, installed runtime and operator-path acceptance independently. Local synthetic authentication proves local persistence/routing; a later real-account canary is a separate authority and evidence gate, not silently replaced with fake-auth success.

The acceptance packet retains build hashes, commands, red/green output, fixture identity, cumulative-accounting invariants, owned-process cleanup and remaining gaps. No full-scope pass is claimed from a version string, nonempty auth file or unit test count.

## Out of Scope

Complete Byobu restore (#368); business/provider experiments; production account login/logout; automatic account substitution; credential copying; governor activation; resource renewal/reset; global WSL shutdown; deleting prior fixture contents; silent live daemon restarts; unrestricted cross-host tenant discovery. These may not be inferred from test setup authorization.

## Further Notes

Approved choices: shared history within a tenant across compatible builds; owner-routed resume; explicit linked successor across accounts; modified default launch; shared supported MCP operator identity; automatic update checks with explicit activation; full available successor history with preserved accounting; existing disposable WSL setup and staged/HDD payload handling.

Current evidence: the original profile authentication regression has not been reproduced. Separate account auth files exist, but validity and account routing are unproven. The fixture is prepared, not acceptance-tested. Existing profile documentation still restricts cross-account concurrency. The running modified native package has independent tests but broader installed acceptance remains incomplete. #369 is coordination; children close only on their own named delivery target.

Definition of done: approved child outcomes delivered through installed paths in the disposable environment, one integrated compatibility/upgrade receipt with explicit remaining live gates, truthful documentation and no automatic production cutover.

items.title: [Research][Node Architect] Bind tool capability/schema identity across discovery and invocation
items.body:
## Paired S1 research record

**Jira:** https://nhatnguyenquang1838.atlassian.net/browse/SCRUM-621  
**Pair state:** `PAIR_SYNCING`  
**Repository:** `nhatnguyenquang1838-coder/gwc`  
**Research snapshot:** `main@bad63d466f3d1e40ee5184d75551c3abaa2f0617`  
**Execution mode:** `chat_connector_only`  
**Boundary:** research/tracking only; no code/branch/PR/merge/deploy/release/production/config/data/secret/migration/destructive action.

## Research Question

How should GWC Node Architect bind the exact tool/connector/MCP capability definition used during discovery and provider planning to the later effectful invocation, so a mutable tool registry, server restart, schema edit, annotation change, or endpoint/profile drift cannot silently reinterpret an already-approved action between `tools/list` and `tools/call` — without duplicating SCRUM-280 capability authorization, SCRUM-382 provider/model substitution, or SCRUM-554 transitive-effect authority?

## REPO EVIDENCE

At exact `main@bad63d466f3d1e40ee5184d75551c3abaa2f0617`, `tools/node_architect/ai_agent_adapter.py` exposes a provider-neutral `Provider.run(pack)` boundary. The shared adapter builds an `InstructionPack`, dispatches it, then checks provider-reported `changed_paths` and `recorded_actions` against path/action allowlists. `authorized_actions` are action-name strings; the reviewed shared path does not bind a tool-registry generation, connector/server endpoint identity, tool-definition digest, `inputSchema`/`outputSchema` digest, annotations digest, or discovery revision to the provider attempt.

Repo evidence:
- https://github.com/nhatnguyenquang1838-coder/gwc/blob/bad63d466f3d1e40ee5184d75551c3abaa2f0617/tools/node_architect/ai_agent_adapter.py
- https://github.com/nhatnguyenquang1838-coder/gwc/blob/bad63d466f3d1e40ee5184d75551c3abaa2f0617/AGENTS.md

## SOURCE EVIDENCE

Current Model Context Protocol documentation defines `tools/list` for discovering tool definitions and `tools/call` for invocation. A tool definition includes `name`, `description`, required `inputSchema`, optional `outputSchema`, annotations and metadata. Servers may advertise `tools.listChanged`; current architecture guidance says clients should request the current tool list when notified of a list change. Current MCP SDK documentation validates invocation arguments against the advertised input schema. Tool annotations are hints, not enforcement, and untrusted-server annotations cannot serve as hard authority.

Sources:
- https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol/blob/main/docs/specification/2026-07-28/schema.mdx
- https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol/blob/main/docs/docs/2026-07-28/learn/architecture.mdx
- https://ts.sdk.modelcontextprotocol.io/v2/get-started/first-client.html
- https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-03-16-tool-annotations/

Context7: `/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol`.

## DEDUPE

`DEDUPE_PASS` after semantic search of BOTH Jira SCRUM and GitHub Issues for tool schema, connector schema, MCP, capability registry, tool drift and adjacent terminology.

Adjacent but non-duplicate:
- `SCRUM-280 / #318`: instruction integrity, untrusted-content confinement and pre-effect capability authorization; not exact mutable tool-definition/registry identity across discovery→invocation.
- `SCRUM-382 / #350`: provider/model substitution compatibility, including tool-profile compatibility; not registry/schema drift during one already-selected execution attempt.
- `SCRUM-554 / #467`: transitive-effect/capability authority; not binding the direct discovered tool definition to call-time identity.
- `SCRUM-616 / #530`: tool schemas as context-window input; not mutable tool-definition identity.
- Jira term search found only unrelated historical Jira-MCP migration work (`SCRUM-70`).

## INFERENCE

1. Tool-name equality is not semantic identity: the same name may keep its string identity while argument schema, output contract, annotations, endpoint/profile or effect semantics change.
2. Repository SHA alone cannot bind external connector/MCP definitions discovered at runtime.
3. `listChanged` is an invalidation/synchronization signal, not a race-free authority proof; correctness must tolerate missed notifications and reconnects.
4. Action allowlisting is necessary but weaker than invocation identity when the mapping from action/tool name to accepted arguments/effects is mutable.
5. Material tool-definition drift is replay-semantic and must be classified before effect.
6. Post-run clean output cannot repair a call made against a materially different tool definition.
7. Tool identity evidence never grants G2–G6 authority.

## PROPOSAL — `ToolCapabilitySnapshot` + `ToolInvocationReceipt`

Snapshot binds at minimum:

```text
schema_version
run_id/task_id/repository/scope_hash
provider_profile_id
tool_server_profile_id
tool_server_profile_digest
protocol_version
registry_generation_or_snapshot_id
tool_name
tool_definition_digest
input_schema_digest
output_schema_digest
annotations_digest
capability_policy_revision
discovered_at
snapshot_digest
```

Invocation receipt binds current definition/schema identities, invocation-request digest, argument-schema validation, revalidation status, result-contract status, typed reasons and receipt digest.

Closed outcomes:

```text
EXACT_TOOL_DEFINITION
BACKWARD_COMPATIBLE_REVALIDATED
MATERIAL_TOOL_DRIFT_REAPPROVAL_REQUIRED
TOOL_DEFINITION_UNAVAILABLE
TOOL_IDENTITY_UNKNOWN
```

Initial effectful/protected path should prefer `EXACT_TOOL_DEFINITION`; future compatibility relaxation must be separately versioned and proven.

Core invariants:

```text
TOOL_INVOCATION_REQUIRES_BOUND_CURRENT_TOOL_DEFINITION
TOOL_NAME_EQUALITY_DOES_NOT_IMPLY_TOOL_SEMANTIC_EQUALITY
INCOMPATIBLE_TOOL_SCHEMA_DRIFT_FAILS_BEFORE_EFFECT
LIST_CHANGED_INVALIDATES_STALE_TOOL_SNAPSHOT
RECONNECT_REQUIRES_TOOL_IDENTITY_REVALIDATION
TOOL_CAPABILITY_EVIDENCE_NEVER_GRANTS_GATE_AUTHORITY
```

## ASSUMPTIONS

1. Discovery exposes sufficient typed metadata for a stable snapshot; unsupported dimensions remain explicit.
2. `listChanged` support is optional, so correctness cannot depend solely on notifications.
3. First slice may require exact digest equality for effectful tools.
4. SCRUM-280 remains the authority ceiling; this contract proves which concrete tool definition that policy is applied to.
5. Server/profile identities can be represented without persisting credentials.
6. Non-MCP connectors may require adapter-specific identity extraction while conforming to one provider-neutral evidence shape.

## RISKS

- Exact pinning may over-block harmless description/metadata edits unless canonical semantics are carefully defined.
- Dynamic registries may not expose explicit generations; snapshot digest may need to supply identity.
- Missed list-change notifications/reconnect can leave stale caches without independent invocation-time revalidation.
- Annotations are hints and can be false.
- Schema equality does not prove implementation/effect equality; server/profile identity and transitive-effect controls remain necessary.
- Tool descriptions may contain untrusted content; SCRUM-280 remains necessary.
- Cross-host serialization differences require the governed canonical digest profile rather than ad-hoc JSON hashing.

## ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

1. Inventory all Node Architect provider/tool/MCP/connector discovery and effectful invocation surfaces.
2. Every covered effectful invocation binds exact server/profile + tool definition + input-schema identity for the current attempt.
3. Same-name changed input schema is detected before invocation and cannot silently execute.
4. `tools/list_changed` or equivalent invalidates stale snapshot evidence; correctness does not depend solely on receiving it.
5. Reconnect/server restart causes identity re-resolution before next effectful call.
6. Arguments are validated against the bound current input schema before effect.
7. Structured result is validated against bound output schema where supplied; unsupported/missing output schema is explicit.
8. Replay uses recorded tool-definition identity rather than silently resolving mutable latest state.
9. Server/profile/tool/schema/annotation drift yields typed exact/compatible/material-drift outcomes; unknown compatibility fails closed/defer.
10. Tests cover same-name schema drift, remove/re-add, listChanged, missed notification, reconnect, server/profile drift, stale cache, malformed args, output mismatch and retry/replay.
11. Evidence excludes secrets/credentials and uses canonical governance serialization/digest semantics.
12. Tool identity/revalidation evidence never grants or substitutes G2/G3/G4/G5/G6 authority.

## OUT OF SCOPE

No implementation/code/branch/PR/merge/deploy/release/production/config/data/secret/migration/destructive action. No replacement of SCRUM-280, SCRUM-382 or SCRUM-554. No requirement for S1 to modify external tool/MCP servers. No claim that annotations are hard security guarantees.

## SELF-REVIEW

The candidate was challenged against #318, #350, #467 and #530 before creation. The proposal narrows the independent TOCTOU question of **which mutable tool definition** a capability decision authorizes at invocation time. `listChanged` is treated as invalidation evidence only. No current malicious server or incident is claimed. Tool identity alone does not prove business correctness/downstream effects. No formal repository validator PASS or CI PASS is claimed.

## THREE-ROUND FUTURE DELIVERY PLAN

**Round 1 — Inventory + contract fixtures:** inventory discovery/invocation routes; define semantic tool canonicalization + schemas; build same-name schema-change/remove-readd/annotation/server-profile/reconnect/missed-notification fixtures; define typed reason taxonomy.

**Round 2 — Discovery binding + invocation revalidation:** bind tool snapshot to provider attempt/replay identity; validate args; re-resolve after listChanged/reconnect/cache/profile drift; emit invocation receipt and compose with SCRUM-280 capability decision.

**Round 3 — Race hardening + conformance + rollout:** change-after-list-before-call/missed-notification/restart/cache/retry churn faults; MCP/provider-independent conformance; exact-head CI plan; one allowlisted pre-prod route; drift/revalidation/schema-mismatch/stale-cache metrics.

items.body:
> **Epic.** Children, demand-gated (all `deferred: no demand`): #52 (sandboxed creator code — the
> long pole) · #53 (curated publish + review) · #54 (automated pre-review safety scanning) ·
> #55 (creator experience) · #56 (cost governance + abuse controls) · #57 (metering → payout-ready).
> Gating prerequisite: **#142** (trust gating before third parties may declare runtime/workflow
> capabilities). Strategy constraint: **#68** (focus bet — 10 external users on ONE runtime agent
> before expanding).
>
> *Each child said only "part of the open-to-third-party program" in prose; they now name this
> issue, and this issue names them.*

## Strategy (updated 2026-08-01)

**Near-term the operator builds the agents himself** — first-party, but **exemplary / reference-quality** so future creators can see them and build similar. The agents mature the platform and seed the eventual catalog + docs.

**Operating principle:** build every agent the *creator way* — as declarative **data** through the platform path (capability registry, tool catalog, surfaces), never bespoke platform code. Every place an agent forces a platform code change = the platform's next feature.

**Sequencing:** do the cheap data-driven foundation now (#51 / PR #59 + declarative schema + a "view/fork source" example gallery). **Defer the expensive marketplace machine — Tier-2 sandbox (#52), review (#53/#54), payouts (#57) — until one/two agents prove people will PAY** (billing is currently deferred; PAS is the paid launch). This epic stays the north star; its expensive parts are demand-gated.

---

Turn PAGS from "first-party agents + curated fleet" into a **creator marketplace**. Target architecture is in \`docs/agent-platform-strategy.md\`; concrete program plan in \`docs/third-party-agents-plan.md\`.

## Owner decisions (2026-08-01)
- **Scope of first release:** Tier-1 declarative config agents **+ Tier-2 sandboxed custom code**.
- **Trust model:** **curated review** — creators submit; every agent/version is reviewed before it's listed.
- **Monetization:** **free/beta first** — open creation now; build payout plumbing behind a flag, launch payouts later.

## The gate
**Do not open publicly until the Tier-2 sandbox (#52) and cost governance (#56) are proven.** Everything else can ship incrementally behind invite/curated.

## Workstreams
- #51 — Tier-1: declarative agent schema + open tool catalog + shared runtime
- #52 — Tier-2: sandboxed creator code via Dynamic Workers **(critical path)**
- #53 — Curated publish + review pipeline
- #54 — Automated pre-review safety scanning
- #55 — Creator experience: onboarding + authoring UI + Coder flywheel
- #56 — Cost governance & abuse controls **(gates the public open)**
- #57 — Metering → payout-ready (payouts behind a flag)

## Phasing
- **Phase 0 — foundation (partly in flight):** admin access-control (#28), metering (#44), usage/spend + kill switch (#39/#46), moderation UI (#41). The safety net that must exist first.
- **Phase 1 — Tier-1 to invited creators:** #51 + #53 + #55 (config-only authoring, curated). Dogfood by migrating repo-chat onto the formal schema.
- **Phase 2 — Tier-2 code (the hard part):** #52 + #54 + #56. Red-team the sandbox before any third party touches it.
- **Phase 3 — widen + monetize:** loosen curation as guardrails mature; flip payouts (#57).

## Prereqs already true
Tenant isolation, envelope crypto, SSRF guard, MCP scopes, per-instance DO isolation (see \`SECURITY.md\`) — the security floor Tier-2 builds on.
