items.body:
# DIVINE SHINE — HARVEY AI ACQUISITION PILOT
**Owner directive | Single engineering coordination issue | 2026-10-31 CT**
**Repository:** MikeSimmonsAI/advisorflow-web
**Drive project:** https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1EZPZCGGtPJ7YOQ9NUccZxswTfDKHUj1Z
**Reference source:** https://github.com/ethanplusai/harvey (MIT; retain notices)

## Mission and boundary
Build one fully functional, polished, PRIVATE EvoSys Pro client-acquisition workspace for **Divine Shine Elite Cleaning**, owned by Ciara, serving Dallas–Fort Worth. The service is a **managed operation (Option A)**: EvoSys Pro researches prospects, operates eligible outreach, follows up, qualifies interested companies and books consultations or walkthroughs. Ciara sees appointments, prospect context, quotes and contract outcomes; she closes deals. **Do not expose campaign/Harvey internals to Ciara.** This is NOT Daniel's Commercial Cleaning Blueprint, and must not modify, share records with, or grant access to that product. No rollout to other tenants or brands.

## Success definition
- Free initial 30-day LIVE pilot, counting from verified activation of real operations, not software development.
- Target 3–5 genuinely qualified booked appointments, **not guaranteed**. Report appointments held, estimate/quote conversion, won recurring accounts and monthly contract value separately.
- Proposed discovery pool 750–1,000 DFW businesses and qualified pool 400–600 are hypotheses, subject to discovery accuracy and responsible sending volume.
- A 'qualified booked appointment' requires demonstrable customer interest in commercial/recurring cleaning and calendar-confirmed availability; scraped business names do not count.
- Free pilot, no automatic subscription/commission, no obligation beyond participation and honest feedback/outcome reporting. Prepare a concise pilot agreement, no invented commitments.

## Ciara's customer profile (from her own message)
Recurring commercial cleaning contracts in DFW. Targets: office buildings, medical and professional facilities, apartment complexes, property-management firms, short-term rental managers. Prioritize attainable smaller commercial clients; distinguish specialized medical cleaning from general offices. Capture her service capabilities, coverage, minimum job value, existing account exclusions, proof of insurance/certifications (only truthful verified claims), travel and appointment availability and quote-to-close feedback. Keep onboarding 8th-grader simple, and do not request personal account passwords.

## Architecture: ADAPT, DO NOT DUMP A SECOND APP
Review Harvey main: collectors/discover.py, collectors/profile.py, collectors/people.py, signals.py, agents/scout.py, writer.py, handler.py, analyst.py, gate.py, untrusted.py, state.py and integrations. Treat third-party content as untrusted. Retain MIT copyright/license notices in substantial reused code. Evaluate maturity/dependencies/security carefully.

Existing EvoSys Pro modules to inspect before designing:
- app/routers/lead_intelligence_router.py, app/models/lead_intel_models.py, app/services/qualification.py, app/services/lead_routing.py
- app/services/workforce/, app/jobs/run_ai_workforce_worker.py, app/services/ai_operations/, app/services/ai_gateway* 
- app/services/sales_suppression.py, app/routers/compliance_router.py, app/services/compliance_service.py, app/services/cadence_service.py, app/routers/auto_send_router.py
- app/services/tenant_scheduling.py, calendar providers, appointment models, existing sales workspace
- frontend React routes, Program Access card, God Mode and existing auth/RBAC
- render.yaml, service-role scheduling, database migrations, resource limits.
**Single EvoSys CRM/source of truth**, scoped to Divine Shine. Do not stand up Harvey's independent SQLite CRM/outbox/dashboard/sender as a competing source. Use bounded queued jobs; do not add a runaway 15-min daemon in the RAM-constrained Render backend. Do not rely on consumer Claude/Codex subscription credentials for a commercial customer SaaS model; evaluate compatible production AI gateway cost/rate limits. No exposure of credentials in GitHub/Drive artifacts.

## Mandatory two surfaces
1. **Owner/God Mode operations:** prospect discovery, evidence-based buying signals, search/provider cost estimate, provenance/confidence, DFW segmentation, verified contacts, dedupe, qualification, outreach drafts, mail health, reply inbox/classifications, appointment routing, AI worker health, spending, usage, job tracing, pause/resume/kill switches, outcome conversion dashboard. No fake numbers or placeholders in shipped operating screens.
2. **Divine Shine client workspace:** branded private Program Access card POST-LOGIN; simple dashboard for leads/interested prospects, appointments, prospect context, attendance/outcomes, quote values, recurring deals, notifications, feedback, profile and limited availability controls. No separate public login, tenant-wide access, or God Mode tools. Clean dark sidebar/light content consistent with approved EvoSys Sales Workspace, mobile-friendly, very easy to use.

## Data lifecycle
Discover business -> inspect/provenance -> dedupe -> score vs Divine Shine ICP -> eligible verified contact -> outreach staged -> deterministic pre-send checks + permissions -> authorized send -> reply intake/dedupe -> classify intent and opt-out -> qualified interest -> existing calendar availability checked live -> book in native scheduler -> Ciara notified -> consult held/no-show -> quote -> won/lost -> ROI.
Maintain auditable states and timestamps, company-level stop-on-reply where appropriate, retry/idempotency, confidence and evidence URL, no unsupported inference presented as verified fact.

## Operating constraints
- Strict single-tenant feature-flag and per-tenant authorization; no interaction with Daniel/SCI/Wholesale/Roofing/BookaBoost data or workflows.
- Practice mode and test fixtures isolated from real customers; no demo/sample data leaks.
- Channel eligibility and suppression checked at execution time; do not confuse lawful B2B email with permission for SMS or AI cold calling. Honor opt-outs; fail closed if eligibility unclear.
- AI does not autonomously choose calendar availability or override suppression. Respect current EvoSys kill switches, tenant budgets, global rate limits and approval configuration.
- No external outreach, customer account provisioning, billing, new paid provider spend, production migrations, or production deployment merely because this issue exists. Code can be developed/tested in isolated branch and PR. Get the existing owner's release/approval workflow satisfied before merge/deploy and controlled pilot activation.
- Store only non-sensitive diagrams/screenshots/docs in project Drive; real lead PII in restricted approved systems. Never post keys, addresses, contact exports or client secrets to public issue.

## Work phases and acceptance gates
**P0 — audit:** inspect current EvoSys and Harvey code, create source-to-target integration matrix; explain 'reuse vs rewrite', licensing, compatibility, email deliverability, data model, hosting/AI/prospect data costs, user roles, and risk list with exact paths and test plan.
**P1 — UX and onboarding:** functional Program Access card after login, approved org-scoped access, owner ops + Ciara simple app, business profile and availability, live truthful counts.
**P2 — discovery:** adapter(s), cost estimate, safe first sample cohort (no sends), signals, evidence, dedupe, qualification and tenant-safe pipeline.
**P3 — conversations:** integrate existing managed email/outreach, inbox/intent, guardrails, follow-ups, cost usage; dry run full state machine first. No silent live send.
**P4 — booking/outcomes:** existing calendar authority, qualified booked/held outcome tracking, notification, estimate/won/lost and reports.
**P5 — launch readiness:** security/RBAC, worker idempotency, memory/load, sending reputation, error/kill switch, real-browser tests, backup/rollback and clear pilot start gating.
**P6 — 30-day pilot:** only after launch approval, monitor verified contact-to-booking funnel and document outcomes; decide expand/no-expand AFTER evidence.

## Single-thread working protocol
Use THIS ISSUE as the permanent project ledger. Start by commenting an exact-time CT architecture audit, files inspected, risks, dependencies, proposed minimal implementation slices, and explicit P0 deliverables. Post timestamped progress and links to commits/PRs/test output/screenshots/Drive artifacts in THIS SAME issue. Avoid new handoff threads. Make a clean isolated branch and targeted PR when ready, with tests and accurate screenshots. Never claim 'live', 'done', or customer contacted without recorded evidence. Do not modify Daniel's blueprint. Keep Program Access simple and avoid 'Control Room' clutter. If unavailable external keys/accounts are needed, proceed with mocks and document the precise blocker rather than stalling the rest.

## Drive
Project: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1EZPZCGGtPJ7YOQ9NUccZxswTfDKHUj1Z
- Scope: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1H9bigM_04Z1B-GWMlZ4koXqJ1G7LeMoG
- Screenshots: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1B3-GXxwcK3jhLlN6nTe0Mq_tvkkR7LrC
- Business profile: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1gRrO01njtQco-1HTvd4zXofVDAGJbN3M
- Research: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1qsABSz_MmeFxiaHXR__z_afGTGM7bVxa
- QA: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/15sjRR83nXZ3rCLSNmHYrJlQJlZbHoaC1

**Owner decision is to proceed with development of this single-company proof, not to enable customer contact or broaden distribution. Begin P0 audit, then P1 implementation within normal engineering gates.**

## Problem

Elsa needs both foundational engine/platform modules and a broad set of business integrations. Developers should be able to work on both in one solution, using solution filters for focused development and debugging. A connector release must not require republishing unrelated connectors or core.

Shared cloud users cannot upload arbitrary NuGet packages. They therefore depend on the supplied capabilities, connection experience, and catalog to build complete business processes. Adding API-call activities alone is insufficient: authentication, trigger lifecycle, tenant isolation, data handling, compatibility, and maintenance must be reusable platform capabilities.

## Outcomes

1. Core, Extensions and Studio are developed in one repository under root siblings `core/`, `extensions/` and `studio/`, each owning its `src/`, `test/` and `docs/`, with a shared root solution and focused solution filters.
2. Connectors have explicit, independent release units and compatibility declarations.
3. Source-based development and published-package compatibility are both verified.
4. Shared infrastructure handles connections, authentication, actions, triggers, files, resilience, and diagnostics.
5. Shared cloud exposes a curated catalog with enforced tenant and capability boundaries.
6. Evidence-based research prioritizes complete customer workflows rather than connector counts.
7. A pilot cohort validates the architecture and provides reusable implementation and contribution patterns.
8. The program is decomposed into Program → Epic → Feature → Story → Task issues, with dependencies and acceptance criteria.

## Scope and constraints

- **Canonical repository:** elsa-workflows/elsa-core. Consolidate all Elsa Extensions and Elsa Studio here, including persistence, scheduling, runtime, expression and integration modules, paired backend/Blazor modules, tests, samples, build assets and relevant documentation. Preserve source history and account for active issues/PRs through an explicit migration ledger. Create new program work here.
- Reuse or link existing issues and implementations instead of duplicating them.
- Preserve existing package IDs, activity identities, serialized contracts, and consumer entry points unless an explicit migration is provided.
- Initially keep engine packages and tightly coupled platform packages in their existing coordinated release groups. Independent connector releases are the first objective.
- Package release, host deployment, and workflow activity/schema versioning are separate concerns.
- Shared hosts initially use a curated, pinned connector set. Arbitrary conflicting connector/dependency versions within one process are out of scope.
- Repository consolidation does not automatically consolidate unrelated commercial products.
- Shared cloud, dedicated deployments, and self-hosting need explicit capability profiles.
- Public issues and artifacts must not contain credentials, private customer correspondence, or confidential demand evidence. Record sanitized findings.
- No schedule, staffing allocation, or demand ranking is established by this charter. Estimate after the inventory and pilots reduce uncertainty.

## Studio inclusion and release boundaries

Include Elsa Studio in the monorepo so backend and Blazor functionality can be developed, debugged, reviewed and tested together. Audit paired modules already in Extensions. Provide focused solutions/filters and sample hosts spanning both sides.

Source co-location does not imply a single release train. Tightly coupled server/Studio module pairs may share a release unit; the Studio shell and unrelated packages retain explicit independent release policies. Add backend API/protocol and package compatibility checks. Preserve existing package identities and source ownership during migration.

### E1 — Integration landscape research and prioritization

**Features**
- F1.1: Establish target personas and workflow scenarios.
- F1.2: Build a broad candidate catalog.
- F1.3: Perform technical/commercial feasibility investigations.
- F1.4: Rank delivery cohorts and define their operation-level scope.

**Research method**
1. Start with the existing extensions inventory and public requests.
2. Identify target scenarios for Microsoft-centric teams, SaaS/business operations, developers, and self-hosted enterprise users.
3. Survey approximately 50–100 candidate services across the categories below. This is a bounded discovery target, not a completeness claim.
4. Deeply investigate the top 15–20 candidates using official provider documentation.
5. Validate demand from authorized evidence and maintainer/customer input. Competitor availability is discovery evidence, not proof of Elsa demand.
6. Produce ranked cohorts, exclusions, unresolved questions, effort ranges, and confidence levels.

**Required catalog fields**
Stable ID, provider, categories, target personas, concrete workflows, existing Elsa status, proposed actions/searches/triggers, authentication types/scopes, OAuth app/verification requirements, API and webhook documentation, polling/renewal requirements, pagination and rate limits, file/size constraints, paid-tier/API-access restrictions, sandbox/test availability, SDK/license considerations, data residency considerations where relevant, maintenance burden, ownership/sponsorship, shared-cloud eligibility, Elsa compatibility, evidence URLs, checked date, confidence, and recommendation.

Use machine-readable records (JSON/YAML or equivalent) plus a generated readable summary. Unknowns remain explicit; do not infer API support from a competitor listing.

**Proposed scoring**
Score 0–5 on each dimension: evidenced demand (30%), complete-workflow coverage (25%), feasibility (15%), shared-infrastructure reuse (15%), and maintenance sustainability (15%; higher means easier to sustain). Publish rationale and confidence separately. Apply hard eligibility checks for usable API/auth access and cloud restrictions; do not let a weighted score conceal blockers. Weights are an initial hypothesis to validate.

**Candidate categories**
- Microsoft: OneDrive, SharePoint, Outlook, Teams, Microsoft calendar, Dynamics 365.
- Google: Drive, Sheets, Gmail, Calendar.
- Communication: Slack, email/SMTP providers, Twilio, Discord, Telegram.
- Finance: Moneybird, Stripe, Exact Online, Xero, QuickBooks, PayPal.
- CRM: HubSpot, Salesforce, Pipedrive, Zoho CRM.
- Engineering: GitHub, Azure DevOps, GitLab, Jira.
- Support: Zendesk, Freshdesk, Intercom.
- Data/storage/messaging: SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL, S3-compatible storage, Azure Blob, Azure Service Bus, RabbitMQ, Kafka.
- Knowledge/tasks: Notion, Airtable, Asana, Trello.
- Commerce/documents: Shopify, WooCommerce, DocuSign and document-processing services.
- AI/agents: model invocation, structured extraction, agent execution, governed remote tools.

### E4 — Connector SDK, connections, and execution infrastructure

**Features**
- F4.1: Tenant-owned named connections and runtime authorization.
- F4.2: OAuth/API-key authentication lifecycle and integration with the existing Elsa Secrets module, subject to the architecture assessment below.
- F4.3: Typed actions/searches, schemas, pagination, and dynamic options.

- F4.5: Managed file references and data transformation primitives.
- F4.6: Governed authenticated API requests for the long tail.

**Key acceptance**
- Workflow definitions contain connection references, not embedded secrets.
- Authorization is enforced on each execution/resumption and on design-time lookups.
- Refresh concurrency, reconnect/revocation, credential rotation, scope changes, and environment promotion are defined.
- Retries distinguish safe reads from writes with unknown outcomes; use provider idempotency where available and never promise universal exactly-once delivery.
- Large files use bounded streams/references with ownership, expiration, quotas, and cleanup.
- Diagnostics redact secrets and expose actionable provider errors.
- Reuse existing Elsa abstractions where suitable. Audit JSON/CSV/XML, date/time, validation, approvals, and subworkflow capabilities before adding replacements.
- Generic authenticated requests enforce provider/destination and credential-forwarding restrictions.

**Exit:** pilot connectors share these capabilities without connector-specific copies of generic lifecycle logic.

### Secrets module and connection architecture decision

Explicitly investigate whether and how integration connections should leverage **Elsa's existing Secrets module**. Reuse is the preferred starting hypothesis, not an assertion that its current implementation already satisfies the requirements.

**Proposed responsibility split to evaluate**
- A connection owns non-secret metadata: provider, account/administration identifiers, granted scopes, status, ownership, and references to credentials.
- The Secrets module or an adapter over its provider abstractions resolves/protects sensitive material: API keys, OAuth client secrets, refresh tokens, access tokens when persisted, and webhook signing secrets.
- The authentication/connection layer coordinates consent, refresh, reconnect, and revocation. Secret storage alone does not implement the OAuth lifecycle.
- Workflows refer to connections; connection records refer to secrets. Avoid exposing raw tokens as normal activity inputs/outputs or persisting them in workflow state, logs, traces, or exports.

**Questions and alternatives for the ADR**
1. Can existing Secrets providers support runtime writes, atomic/versioned updates, deletion, and the access patterns needed by rotating OAuth credentials, or are some providers read-only configuration sources?
2. Compare direct reuse, extending Secrets, and a dedicated credential lifecycle store backed by Secrets/provider abstractions. Justify any separate store and avoid duplicating secret management without a demonstrated requirement.
3. Decide whether short-lived access tokens should be cached only or persisted; define expiry, cache isolation/invalidation, and durable refresh-token storage.
4. Define concurrency and recovery for refresh-token rotation across workers, including a crash between provider refresh and local persistence. Do not assume cross-system atomicity.
5. Distinguish platform-owned OAuth application credentials from tenant-owned connection credentials; define authorization for creating, using, sharing, inspecting metadata, rotating, and deleting them.
6. Assess encryption/key management and supported external vault integration from actual module capabilities. Define outage behavior, audit events without secret values, and least-privilege access.
7. Define secret reference/version semantics, environment-specific binding during promotion, disconnect/revocation, tenant deletion, and cleanup of credentials shared by multiple connections.
8. Verify background polling, webhook renewal, and resumed workflows resolve credentials through an authorized tenant execution context.

**Deliverables and acceptance**
- E0 audit documents actual Secrets APIs/providers and gaps.
- E4 produces an ADR comparing alternatives and selecting a supported approach before credential persistence is implemented.
- Create feature/story/task issues for reuse, necessary module extensions/adapters, and any credential migration.
- A pilot demonstrates connection creation, authorized credential resolution, token refresh/rotation, reconnect/revocation, and redacted diagnostics.
- E6 verifies cross-tenant access denial, export/state redaction, concurrent refresh behavior, storage failure handling, and disconnect/deletion semantics.
- Record how the chosen approach applies to self-hosted deployments and preserves existing Secrets consumers.

### E5 — Durable triggers and event lifecycle

**Features**
- F5.1: Webhook routing, verification, subscription provisioning, and renewal.
- F5.2: Durable polling with cursors, leases, pagination, and fair scheduling.
- F5.3: Deduplication, durable ingestion, recovery, and operational health.

**Key acceptance**
- Tenant routing uses trusted subscription/connection records rather than trusting payload tenant IDs.
- Events are acknowledged according to a documented durable-ingestion policy.
- Duplicate/reordered events, missed renewal, crash/restart, invalid signatures, and provider downtime have defined handling.
- Workflow publish/unpublish, connection revocation, and tenant deletion reconcile subscriptions and polling jobs.
- Delivery guarantees and reconciliation behavior are explicit; deduplication is not described as exactly-once external side effects.
- Health signals identify stalled polling, expired subscriptions, lag, and repeated failures.

**Exit:** webhook and polling scenarios survive restart, isolation, duplicate-delivery, and renewal tests.

### E6 — Shared-cloud policy, isolation, and operational readiness

**Features**
- F6.1: Shared/dedicated/self-hosted capability profiles.
- F6.2: Tenant isolation and outbound network policy.
- F6.3: Quotas, fairness, observability, and failure containment.
- F6.4: Curated host composition, upgrades, rollback, and deprecation.

**Key acceptance**
- Shared cloud accepts curated packages only.
- Connections, caches, files, webhook mappings, polling state, logs, and quotas are tenant-scoped and tested.
- HTTP/database/remote-tool capabilities address SSRF, private-network access, redirects, credential leakage, and resource exhaustion.
- Expressions and scripts have an assessed execution boundary; language-engine configuration is not assumed to be a security sandbox.
- Host manifests pin the tested connector set. Do not promise per-tenant arbitrary package versions in one process.
- Upgrade tests cover saved definitions and suspended workflows; incompatible changes require documented migration or routing to compatible hosts.
- Connection/provider outages are observable without exposing secrets.

**Exit:** the pilot cohort meets the shared-cloud policy and has deploy/rollback and incident runbooks.

## Risks and decisions to record

- Monorepo builds may become expensive: dependency-aware CI and focused filters.
- Shared infrastructure changes may create release coupling: keep contracts narrow and validate consumers.
- NuGet/API compatibility may differ from source compatibility: test exact artifacts and supported host combinations.
- Provider OAuth verification/API access may block delivery: investigate early.
- Long-running workflows may break on schema/type changes: stable identities and explicit migration policy.
- Broad connector coverage may exceed maintenance capacity: narrow operation scope, ownership, cohorts, and deprecation.
- Scripts/HTTP/remote tools can bypass intended tenant boundaries: enforce capability and execution policies.
- Cloud data models may already provide connection/secret functionality: inventory and reuse before introducing competing abstractions.
- Generated OpenAPI wrappers may accelerate implementation but do not solve auth, lifecycle, UX, or semantics: evaluate selectively.
- Research must distinguish verified facts, assumptions, and demand hypotheses.

Required ADRs: repository migration; release-unit/versioning policy; package compatibility; connection/secret ownership and existing Secrets-module reuse versus extension; trigger lifecycle/delivery guarantees; shared-cloud capability policy; host upgrade/workflow compatibility; Elsa 4 reuse boundary.

items.title: Living Knowledge Graph — auto-map the tenant's brain after each new data source
items.body:
# The Living Knowledge Graph — Argus's Growing Brain

This is the right instinct. You're describing what Argus actually needs to **understand** a company, not just monitor it. The metaphor is perfect: a brain where each new entity is a neuron, each relationship a synapse, and the whole thing grows denser and smarter over time.

## The Mental Model

Think of three layers stacked on top of each other:

1. **SEMANTIC LAYER**: *"What does this mean?"* Concepts · Goals · Themes · Patterns (LLM-generated, abstract)
2. **ENTITY LAYER**: *"Who/what exists?"* Customers · Employees · Deals · Products · Vendors (extracted from data, concrete)
3. **RAW LAYER**: *"What happened?"* Rows · Documents · Events · Messages (ingested verbatim, immutable)

## Step 1: The Entity Discovery Pipeline

When new data lands, Argus follows this flow:

- **Schema Mapper**: For structured sources (DBs, sheets).
- **Entity Extractor**: LLM extracts entities + properties (e.g., *"Acme Corp is a customer, ARR 240K"*).
- **Resolver**: Deduplication using fuzzy match + embedding similarity.
- **Relationship Inferer**: Infers connections to existing graph (e.g., *"John Smith works at Acme"*).
- **Graph Writer**: Persists nodes + edges and emits a *"new neuron"* event.

## Step 2: The Graph Itself

Use a **property graph model**. Implementation can be simple Postgres tables for v1:

- **Nodes Table**: ID, Type, Name, Properties (JSONB), Embedding (Vector), Confidence, etc.
- **Edges Table**: ID, From_Node, To_Node, Relation, Properties, Evidence, etc.

## Step 3: Schema-Free, Type-Discovered

Don't predefine all entity types. Let Argus discover them. Start with a seed ontology and let the LLM propose new types/relations after they appear consistently in the data.

## Step 4: Entity Resolution

Use three-stage matching to avoid garbage data:

- **Exact match**: Strong identifiers (email, phone).
- **Fuzzy match**: Names + context.
- **Embedding match**: Vector similarity judged by LLM.

## Step 5: Relationship Inference

Move beyond direct data to inferred intelligence:

- **Transitive**: A works at B, B is a subsidiary of C → A works for C.
- **Temporal**: Engagement drops over time → Relationship likely shifted.
- **Behavioral/Structural**: Identifying high-intent actions or network connectors.

## Step 6: The "New Neuron Born" Event

Make growth visible. High-novelty + high-significance events become brief items.
> *"Argus discovered a pattern: 4 of your last 7 customers came from healthcare."*

## Step 7: Multi-Hop Reasoning (GraphRAG)

The combination of graph traversal + vector similarity + LLM reasoning allows Argus to answer complex questions like *"Why did Q2 margin drop?"* by walking through deals, products, partners, and news.

## Step 8: Decay, Pruning, and Forgetting

Keep the graph intelligent by dropping confidence in unconfirmed edges and archiving low-value/inactive branches.

## Step 9: The Three Storage Layers

- **Graph** (Relational): Postgres/Neo4j.
- **Vector** (Similarity): pgvector/Qdrant.
- **Warehouse** (Analytical): ClickHouse/DuckDB.

## The Strategic Moat

The company-specific knowledge graph built over months is **non-replicable**. It makes the product "sticky" because the graph is the company's brain sitting on your platform. Build a simple visualization for the CEO to make this value tangible.

---

# Proposed implementation — surprise edition

Below is the build plan I'd actually ship. The brief is good; the surprises are in how this plugs into the architecture we already have ([`ARCHITECTURE_TARGET.md`](../blob/main/docs/ARCHITECTURE_TARGET.md), [`AGENT_LOOPS.md`](../blob/main/docs/AGENT_LOOPS.md), [`STRATEGY.md`](../blob/main/docs/STRATEGY.md)) and where I'd deviate from the brief to make it cheaper to build and harder to break.

## 0. Reframing — the graph is *not* a separate product

The KG is not "another store." It's the **deduplicated, typed, evidenced index** of the same rows the Data Plane already holds. Every node and edge **must** trace back to a query receipt (the same trust pipeline as memos — see L3 Critic in [`AGENT_LOOPS.md`](../blob/main/docs/AGENT_LOOPS.md)). If you can't click a node and see the SQL that proved it exists, it doesn't belong in the graph.

This single rule kills 80 % of the "graph is wrong" failure modes that plague GraphRAG demos.

## 1. Tables (Postgres + pgvector, no Neo4j in v1)

```sql
-- one shared schema per tenant Data Plane
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;

CREATE TABLE kg_node (
  id           bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id    bigint NOT NULL,
  type         text   NOT NULL,         -- 'customer','employee','vendor','deal',...
  name         text   NOT NULL,
  canonical_key text,                   -- email|phone|vat_id when available
  props        jsonb  NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'::jsonb,
  embedding    vector(1536),
  confidence   real   NOT NULL DEFAULT 1.0,
  evidence_count int  NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  first_seen   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  last_seen    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  decayed_at   timestamptz,
  UNIQUE (tenant_id, type, canonical_key)
);
CREATE INDEX kg_node_name_trgm ON kg_node USING gin (name gin_trgm_ops);
CREATE INDEX kg_node_emb       ON kg_node USING ivfflat (embedding vector_cosine_ops);

CREATE TABLE kg_edge (
  id          bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id   bigint NOT NULL,
  src         bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES kg_node(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  dst         bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES kg_node(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  relation    text   NOT NULL,         -- 'works_at','owns','paid_by','ships_to'
  props       jsonb  NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'::jsonb,
  confidence  real   NOT NULL DEFAULT 1.0,
  evidence_count int NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  first_seen  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  last_seen   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (tenant_id, src, dst, relation)
);

-- the trust spine: every node and every edge must point to at least one receipt
CREATE TABLE kg_evidence (
  id          bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  node_id     bigint REFERENCES kg_node(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  edge_id     bigint REFERENCES kg_edge(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  receipt_id  bigint NOT NULL,         -- FK to query_receipts (the SQL that proved it)
  extractor   text   NOT NULL,         -- 'schema_mapper','llm_extractor','inferer'
  confidence  real   NOT NULL,
  raw_row_ref jsonb,                   -- {table:..., pk:..., col:...} for the source cell
  CHECK ((node_id IS NULL) <> (edge_id IS NULL))
);
```

> No Neo4j in v1. Recursive CTEs and `JSON_AGG` handle 3-5 hop traversal under 50 ms for ≤1 M-node tenants. We add Neo4j the day a real customer breaks Postgres, not before. Same posture as in [`ARCHITECTURE.md`](../blob/main/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) on infra.

## 2. The discovery pipeline — wired into the existing connector

The `Connector` interface in [`ARCHITECTURE_TARGET.md`](../blob/main/docs/ARCHITECTURE_TARGET.md) already has `introspect()` and `sample()`. Extend it with a single new capability:

```ts
// packages/connectors/src/types.ts
interface KnowledgeExtractor {
  extractEntities(opts: { batchRows: Row[]; tableHint: string }): Promise<EntityCandidate[]>;
  extractRelations(opts: { node: Node; nearby: Node[] }): Promise<RelationCandidate[]>;
}
```

When a connector is created, the existing crawl job (`packages/investigators/src/agents/runtime.ts` already has the seed) gains an extra stage:

```
introspect → sample → ⟨ NEW ⟩ kg_extract → analyze → emit_neuron_event
```

The `kg_extract` stage is an L1-style deterministic-correction loop:

```
1. SchemaMapper: for each table, decide its likely entity_type
                 from column hints + name (rule-based first, LLM fallback).
2. RowExtractor: for the top N rows, ask an LLM tool-use to emit
                 typed entities. Reject any entity not citing a row.
3. Resolver:     pgvector + trigram + LLM-judged final tiebreak.
4. EdgeInferer:  only edges with two evidence-bearing endpoints
                 and an FK / co-occurrence signal.
5. Writer:       upsert; emit 'neuron.born' if novel.
```

## 3. The "first 30 minutes" surprise — Cold Start Spike + Drip Enrichment

When a new connector is created, run **two phases**, not one:

| Phase | When | What | LLM cost target |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cold Start Spike** | First 30 min after connection | Heavy extraction pass on the top ~50 tables × ~500 rows each. Bootstraps the entire entity layer in one burst. | $5–15 one-time |
| **Drip Enrichment** | Ongoing, hourly | Process only the rows whose `updated_at > last_drip_at`. Cheap. Keeps the graph current without re-paying the cold-start cost. | <$0.50/day |

The CEO sees a populated graph within 30 minutes of "Connect DB." That's the wow moment. The drip keeps it fresh forever. Most KG systems either drip forever (slow start) or full-rebuild nightly (expensive forever) — neither gives you both fast onboarding and cheap steady state.

## 4. New-neuron events — make growth a delivery channel, not a side-effect

We already deliver to Slack/email/Discord (see [`docs/EVENTS.md`](../blob/main/docs/EVENTS.md)). Add a new channel template:

```
🧠 Argus learned something
   New entity type: HEALTHCARE_CUSTOMER (4 instances)
   First detected: Acme Health on 2026-05-12 from finance_expediteurinvoice
   Why it matters: 4 of your last 7 acquisitions are in this segment.
   See receipts: …
```

These are low-frequency, high-signal pushes. **Throttle to ≤1 per tenant per week** by default — otherwise people learn to ignore them.

## 5. The deviation I'd push back on

The brief proposes "schema-free, type-discovered" from day 0. I'd phase this:

| Day | Strategy | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | **Seeded ontology**: 12 core types (customer, employee, deal, vendor, product, invoice, parcel, shipment, payment, address, account, document) | Demos work immediately; no "the LLM hallucinated 47 entity types" rabbit hole |
| 7 | **LLM-proposed types**, gated by `evidence_count ≥ 5 AND distinct_source_tables ≥ 2` | New types only promoted when the data actually supports them |
| 30 | **Cross-tenant type harvesting** — anonymized type ontologies merged into the catalog | Year-2 moat from [`STRATEGY.md §9`](../blob/main/docs/STRATEGY.md) |

Pure schema-free from day 0 is a known failure mode. Most GraphRAG demos that "discover entities" end up with `Thing`, `Object`, `Item`, `Entity`, and `Stuff` as their top 5 types after a week.

## 6. The semantic layer ↔ knowledge graph duality

[`ARCHITECTURE_TARGET.md §3`](../blob/main/docs/ARCHITECTURE_TARGET.md) ships a semantic layer (canonical concepts mapped to tenant schema). The KG is its dynamic cousin (concrete instances discovered over time). They feed each other:

- **KG → Semantic layer**: when the graph keeps seeing a recurring entity property (e.g., `shipper_type` clusters customers into 3 stable groups), the system **proposes** a new Concept for the semantic layer. The CEO approves it once; every playbook now has access.
- **Semantic layer → KG**: when the user maps `Revenue` to `finance_expediteurinvoice.total_amount`, the entity extractor already knows that `business_id` columns are `Customer` foreign keys. Saves re-discovering it.

This bidirectional loop is the real moat. The longer the graph runs, the more the semantic layer self-completes.

## 7. Decay and pruning — tied to playbook outcomes (not just time)

The brief proposes time-based decay. Better: **outcome-weighted decay**.

```python
def decay_edge(edge, playbook_runs_using_it):
    if any(r.finding_validated_by_user for r in playbook_runs_using_it):
        edge.confidence = min(1.0, edge.confidence + 0.05)   # reinforced
    elif any(r.finding_rejected_by_user for r in playbook_runs_using_it):
        edge.confidence *= 0.5                                # punished
    elif edge.last_seen < now - 90d and edge.evidence_count < 3:
        edge.confidence *= 0.9                                # gentle staleness
    if edge.confidence < 0.1:
        archive(edge)
```

This wires the graph into the L4 meta-loop from [`AGENT_LOOPS.md`](../blob/main/docs/AGENT_LOOPS.md). CEO feedback already tunes playbook priors; the same feedback should tune the graph. Two birds, one signal stream.

## 8. The visualization — radial, not force-directed

For the CEO surface, do **not** ship a generic Neo4j-style force graph. Nobody can read those. Ship a **radial "you are here" view** centred on the asking entity, with concentric rings = hop distance and edge thickness = confidence × usage_recency. Click any node to recenter. The user navigates her business like a map.

A force-directed view goes in the dev/debug screen only.

## 9. Phased delivery

| Phase | Scope | Definition of done |
|---|---|---|
| **P0** (week 1) | Schema + tables, evidence FK to receipts | A migration ships; manual inserts work end-to-end |
| **P1** (weeks 2-3) | Schema mapper + row extractor for Postgres connector, seeded ontology | First DB → first 1k entities + 5k edges, all with receipts |
| **P2** (week 4) | Resolver (3-stage) + Cold-Start Spike vs Drip orchestration | New connector hits 30-min cold-start budget reliably |
| **P3** (weeks 5-6) | Relationship inferer (transitive only first) + neuron-event delivery | Slack channel posts one curated discovery per tenant per week |
| **P4** (weeks 7-8) | Outcome-weighted decay + radial CEO viz | A CEO can navigate their company; rejected edges fade within a week |
| **P5** (later) | Multi-hop GraphRAG into the Composer (L3 Composer in `AGENT_LOOPS.md`) | Memos cite graph paths, not just rows |
| **P6** (later) | Cross-tenant anonymized type harvesting (the Year-2 moat) | New tenants bootstrap with industry-conditioned ontologies |

## 10. The single most underrated piece

The thing the brief doesn't emphasize enough: **evidence_count as a first-class column.** An edge isn't just "true or false"; it's "we've seen this in 47 rows across 3 tables over 5 months." That count is what makes the graph trustworthy and what lets us decay confidently. Every other GraphRAG system I've seen treats edges as Boolean. They aren't. Build the count column on day 0, query against it everywhere, and the system will be self-explaining.

---

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Migration `0006_knowledge_graph.sql` ships with the three tables above
- [ ] `Connector` interface gains `extractEntities()` and `extractRelations()`
- [ ] Cold-Start Spike completes in <30 min on a 100k-row tenant DB with cost <$15
- [ ] Every node/edge has at least one `kg_evidence` row pointing to a `query_receipt`
- [ ] Drip enrichment hourly job stays <$0.50/day on a 100k-row tenant DB
- [ ] Radial CEO viz works for ≤2k visible nodes (lazy-load the rest)
- [ ] Decay job runs nightly and archives edges with confidence <0.1
- [ ] "Neuron born" Slack event delivers at ≤1/week per tenant by default

## Related docs

- [`docs/ARCHITECTURE_TARGET.md`](../blob/main/docs/ARCHITECTURE_TARGET.md) — three-plane architecture this plugs into
- [`docs/AGENT_LOOPS.md`](../blob/main/docs/AGENT_LOOPS.md) — L1/L2/L3/L4 loops the KG feeds and is fed by
- [`docs/STRATEGY.md`](../blob/main/docs/STRATEGY.md) — Year-2 moat (cross-tenant patterns) this enables
- [`docs/INVESTIGATORS.md`](../blob/main/docs/INVESTIGATORS.md) — existing investigator runtime to integrate with

items.title: [FC-03][P0] Normalize versioned product catalogs and capabilities
items.body:
## Triage record

- **Stable key:** FC-03
- **Owner role:** Creative and fulfillment; reviewer: print-production owner. Named owner/reviewer remain kickoff decisions.
- **Priority:** P0 — Catalog differences and changes can invalidate artifacts or quote assumptions.
- **Required for v1:** Yes, mock + selected sandbox release; live excluded.
- **Status:** Planned; backlog only.

## Current evidence

Inspected live GitHub 2026-10-10 at main [4c78849754ed542ca77d3b5e1831f8773f9b54b4](https://github.com/Jevelopers-neatHack-2026/fulfillment-connectors/commit/4c78849754ed542ca77d3b5e1831f8773f9b54b4). The complete tree contains only README.md, docs/architecture/OWNERSHIP.md and ACCEPTANCE.md; all three were read. No AGENTS.md, runtime, lockfile, tests, workflows, adapters or migrations exist. README explicitly says documentation baseline only. Existing #1 is WP08; merged documentation PR #2 verifies no implementation. Acceptance remains planned.

## Scope / non-goals

Normalize one launch product plus extensible provider-specific capabilities. Provider remains catalog authority; connector exposes capability inputs to quoting and preflight.

## Acceptance IDs and expected outcome

Mapping: FC-03.1–3. Local cases supplement original global procedures.

Immutable versioned capability snapshots with provider source refs, additive schema migration and cache invalidation. Never rewrite approval-bound old snapshots.

## Executable validation

Use two incompatible synthetic catalogs and selected sandbox product fixture. Change dimensions, SKU availability, options, destination and shipping between versions; assert stale/unsupported paths block and old evidence remains reproducible.

```sh
./scripts/verify-fulfillment --suite catalog --mode simulated --evidence-dir evidence/FC-03
```

## Required evidence for closure

Capability/spec fixtures, freshness/invalidation report and print-production compatibility review.

Closure requires reviewed implementation links, exact component SHAs and contract/runtime versions, actual commands and exit results, sanitized fixtures/assertions, relevant trace/attempt/artifact references, and explicit environment plus billing_mode (simulated/sandbox/live). Keep full addresses, contact details, secrets, auth tokens, signed asset URLs and raw provider errors out of public evidence. Missing evidence stays pending. items.title: Feature: Backplane NATS publisher for async-task MCP tools
items.body:
## Why

EA async demos require IDE → MCP tool → backplane envelope → DGX zelosclient → vLLM → reply. Today zelosmcp has no async-task tools. Without this, the async demo paths (`zelosai#44 / #47 / #50`) cannot route through zelosmcp at all — they would have to bypass it and go straight to the gateway, which contradicts the v1 surface in `zelosai/docs/architecture/00-overview.md`.

## Files to change

- `src/zelosmcp/tools/async_task.py` — MCP tool: `submit_inference_task(prompt, model, params) -> {id, replyTopic}`. Constructs an envelope (correlation-id, subject, scopes, payload) and publishes to `inference.requests.<tenant>.<class>` on NATS.
- `src/zelosmcp/backplane/__init__.py` — new package.
- `src/zelosmcp/backplane/publisher.py` — async NATS publisher (`nats-py`), reuses connection across invocations.
- `src/zelosmcp/backplane/envelope.py` — Pydantic envelope schema, must match the schema in `ZelosAI/zelosbackplane` v0.3 validation feature.
- `tests/test_async_task.py` — embedded NATS test server + assertion that publishing produces the expected subject + payload.

## Verification

- Unit tests green against `nats-server` in test mode.
- Against a running backplane: `submit_inference_task` succeeds; backplane logs show the envelope received on the expected topic.
- Reply-topic round-trip end-to-end: invoke → wait for reply on `<replyTopic>` → assert envelope shape.

## Decisions

- NATS subjects shaped as `inference.requests.<tenant>.<class>` per `zelosbackplane#11`. Multi-tenant deferred — EA uses `default` tenant.
- Replies use a per-request inbox (`_INBOX.<uuid>`) rather than a shared reply subject, simplifying correlation.
- Envelope schema is shared with backplane's v0.3 validation issue — both repos must reference the same Pydantic source; for EA we duplicate, schema library is a v1.0 item.

## Dependencies

- This-repo broker HTTP+WS client (A.2) merged first — shared connection-management patterns.
- `ZelosAI/zelosbackplane#11` (NATS connector) merged.
- Backplane v0.3 envelope schema validation issue merged so schemas align.

Blocks: any EA async demo that routes via zelosmcp (the three demo issues route via gateway today; this issue gives the option to route via mcp instead, which the v1 surface in `00-overview.md` calls out).

---

**Priority:** P1  
**Release:** v0.3  
**Work type:** Feature

items.body:
<!-- gaia-grooming:start -->
## Grooming — next bounded slice

_Codex grooming · 2026-09-05T02:19:52Z. Planning assessment, not live lane status or implementation proof. P1 = delivery/reliability first; P2 = enabling work; P3 = exploration._

- **Assessment / priority:** NEEDS_TRIAGE — advisory-only pilot · P2.
- **Outcome:** Consume one IX advisory package without making Gaia depend on IX availability.
- **Next slice:** Choose one offline metric use case and exact batch; compare its recommendation with a simple baseline.
- **Completion proof:** Wrong digest/stale package is refused; IX absent leaves Gaia working; useful result is reproducible.
- **Ownership:** GitHub assignee: none. Active execution owner not verified; intake must bind an exact lane and reporting owner.
- **Relations:** #49 scope; #89 supplies measurements; #86 may later consume recommendations; TARS remains a distinct payload.
- **Proposed boundaries:** port, adapter-in, projection. One vertical outcome; these are not separate layer-based tasks.
- **Sizing / uncertainty:** M / medium. Uncalibrated focused-effort range: **1–3 h for the next slice only**, excluding queue, CI and independent review; not a delivery deadline.
- **Constraint / correction:** No new model, vector database or network connector is required for the first pilot.

**Admission:** before execution, confirm current code/evidence, one owner, prerequisites and an accepted token/spend cap; create a linked Draft PR when code work starts. Tokens/cost: **UNKNOWN** until provider/model and bounded mandate are selected. No new paid service, installation, credential or authority is granted by this grooming.

Existing acceptance below is retained. Proposed reductions are not permission to close the whole issue after only the next slice; confirm the final scope at intake.
<!-- gaia-grooming:end -->

---

## What

Define optional, organization-neutral **External Intelligence Adapters** for IX and TARS. Start with immutable offline artifact exchange and preserve a stable Seam that can later support automated Connectors without making Gaia depend on either sibling repository at build time, runtime, or availability time.

## Why

IX can provide offline graph, routing, performance, and coordination metrics. TARS can provide theoretical validation, metacognitive critique, invariants, contradictions, and counterexamples. Gaia should consume this intelligence without giving an advisory producer assignment, effect, review, merge, credential, or policy authority.

## Owner and reporting

- **Owner:** unassigned until claimed
- **Reports to:** organization-neutral adoption #49
- **Related registry:** #75
- **Related adaptive routing:** #86
- **Related durable evidence:** #50
- **State:** queued for grooming

## Domain language

- **Advisory Package:** immutable, schema-validated evidence envelope produced outside Gaia and imported without authority.
- **Metric Package:** IX-specific Advisory Package containing offline analytics, confidence, limitations, and Policy Candidates.
- **Validation Package:** TARS-specific Advisory Package containing invariants, critiques, contradictions, counterexamples, confidence, and limitations.
- **External Intelligence Adapter:** implementation at Gaia's offline intelligence Seam that publishes bounded evidence batches and reads Advisory Packages.
- **Connector:** optional transport/availability automation around an Adapter. It never changes the Adapter's authority.
- **Policy Candidate:** advisory proposed policy change that requires simulation, canary, independent review, and an admitted Gaia definition before activation.

## Shared envelope

Every Advisory Package declares:

- producer identity and producer version;
- package kind and schema version;
- source batch identity and content digest;
- observation window and repository/organization scope;
- generated-at, expires-at, and freshness policy;
- algorithm/model/configuration identity;
- confidence and uncertainty representation;
- limitations, missing data, and known invalid domains;
- evidence references and deterministic package digest;
- supersession link when replacing a prior package.

The envelope is shared. IX and TARS payload schemas remain distinct and cannot be forced into one universal score or verdict.

## Initial exchange

1. Gaia publishes a bounded immutable observation batch and manifest to an authorized durable location.
2. IX or TARS consumes the batch offline.
3. The producer publishes one immutable Advisory Package bound to the exact batch digest.
4. Gaia validates identity, schema, digest, scope, freshness, and limitations.
5. Evidence Intake emits `ACCEPTED`, `STALE`, `MISMATCHED`, `CORRUPT`, `UNSUPPORTED`, or `EXPECTED_NONE`.
6. Accepted packages enter an Evidence Funnel as advisory evidence only.

Conceptual Adapter Interface:

- `publishEvidenceBatch(reference)`
- `readAdvisoryPackage(reference)`

Do not add a network Connector until offline exchange and a second Adapter prove the Seam.

## IX responsibilities

- graph and topology analytics;
- capability/task affinity and longitudinal performance metrics;
- coordination-friction and bottleneck detection;
- cluster/shard proposals;
- ETA, cost, and success-probability calibration;
- routing, split/coalesce, and policy candidates with confidence and falsifiers.

## TARS responsibilities

- theory and contract validation;
- metacognitive critique and alternative hypotheses;
- invariant extraction and counterexamples;
- contradiction detection across artifacts or proposed abstractions;
- residual-risk and missing-assumption reports.

Neither producer owns Gaia transitions.

## Availability and failure contract

- Gaia starts, pumps, replays, and recovers with IX and TARS absent.
- Missing packages produce `EXPECTED_NONE` or conservative `UNKNOWN(reason)`, not failure or fabricated evidence.
- Stale, future, corrupt, wrong-tenant, wrong-repository, wrong-batch, or unsupported packages fail closed.
- Conflicting IX/TARS packages remain typed disagreement; Gaia does not resolve truth by majority vote.
- Connector outage cannot block already-admissible local work unless an explicit policy declares the advisory package a human-approved prerequisite.
- No prompts, stdout, credentials, secrets, or sensitive payloads enter the durable package.

## Policy-learning guardrails

An IX or TARS Policy Candidate follows:

`OFFLINE_REPLAY -> SIMULATION -> INDEPENDENT_REVIEW -> BOUNDED_CANARY -> ACCEPTED | REJECTED | ROLLED_BACK`

Use holdouts or baseline comparison, explicit budget, rollback thresholds, and versioned receipts. The candidate cannot self-approve or mutate the routing policy.

## Tracer-bullet acceptance criteria

- [ ] Gaia exports one deterministic evidence batch and manifest without importing IX or TARS code.
- [ ] One IX Metric Package and one TARS Validation Package validate through the shared envelope and distinct payload schemas.
- [ ] Deleting local state and rebuilding from durable GitHub/object references reproduces identical package status.
- [ ] Absence, staleness, wrong digest, wrong tenant/repository, corruption, and unsupported versions yield typed outcomes with zero control effects.
- [ ] Conflicting advisory results reach one evidence funnel without majority-vote truth or hidden coercion.
- [ ] One bounded Policy Candidate is replayed and rejected or canaried without modifying the root authority contract.
- [ ] An in-memory/offline fixture and one real producer package prove the Seam before a network Connector is added.
- [ ] DuckDB projects package freshness, latency, confidence, disagreement, cost, downstream use, and proven policy impact; it remains rebuildable and non-authoritative.

## Rejection criteria

Reject the design if Gaia imports sibling runtime code, requires sibling availability, accepts an opaque scalar as authority, gives a Connector effect permissions, conflates IX and TARS payloads, stores secrets/prompts, or lets stale advisory evidence block unrelated admissible work.

## Delivery slices

1. Shared Advisory Package envelope and validator plus IX/TARS payload schemas.
2. Deterministic offline export/import fixtures and typed refusal outcomes.
3. One real IX Metric Package and one real TARS Validation Package.
4. Evidence Funnel disagreement handling and DuckDB projections.
5. Policy Candidate replay/canary contract.
6. Optional transport Connectors only after the offline Seam is proven.

- The offline trust-manifest signer/verifier slice was extracted into PR #329, based directly on current main: https://github.com/elsaadani40-pixel/Orient/pull/329. It contains seven files and has exact-head Strict CI, Browser Acceptance, CodeQL, and Secret Scanning green. It remains Draft/unmerged.
- PR #312 is another stale persistence branch: 48 files, 3,627 additions, 186 commits; it overlaps PR #319 in nine files, PR #187 in eleven, and PR #188 in fifteen. It changes MemoryService to async and attempts to route JSON/SQLite/PostgreSQL memory through one adapter. It must be reconciled/decomposed rather than merged as a monolith.
- PR #317 now provides a current-main provider/idempotency inventory. PR #330 canonical execution identity is CI-green but unmerged. PR #331 is adding a production shutdown composition integration proof; CI is pending.
- Production async workers remain disabled under issue #189.

## Dependency and overlap map

| Capability | Current candidate | Dependency / conflict |
|---|---|---|
| Offline trust manifest signing/verifying | PR #329 | Extracted from PR #319; seven-file slice; exact-head checks green |
| PostgreSQL optional persistence, migrations, RLS, role provisioning | Remaining PR #319 | Overlaps PR #312 and approval/persistence code; must be split and reviewed independently |
| Unified JSON/SQLite/PostgreSQL memory service | PR #312 | Requires async MemoryService contract migration and adapter transaction semantics; overlaps #319/#188/#187 |
| Gateway identity + fixed read-only execution handler | Remaining PR #319 | Keep separate from mutating tool adapters |
| Trusted evidence ledger | Remaining PR #319 | Depends on canonical evidence record; PR #329 supplies the manifest signer/verifier subset only |
| Root transition/recovery and external anchors | Remaining PR #319 | Separate threat model and recovery proof required |
| S3 Object Lock/Terraform adapters | Remaining PR #319 | Code-only until separately authorized; no cloud apply |
| Async worker/public task lifecycle | PR #188 / issues #185 and #189 | Must remain disabled until provider/local reconciliation and production shutdown gates are proven |

## Required work

1. **Keep PR #329 isolated.** Review the seven-file trust-manifest slice independently; do not merge PR #319 as a monolith.
2. **Choose one canonical memory-persistence design.** Compare PR #312's async service contract and SQLite/PostgreSQL transaction boundaries with current main, PR #319, and PR #188. Do not mix synchronous JSON APIs with asynchronous database adapters.
3. **Split persistence changes into independently testable slices:**
   - memory service async contract + adapter selection;
   - PostgreSQL memory/audit repositories, migrations, and tenant RLS;
   - SQLite memory/audit transaction semantics and crash recovery;
   - migration CLI and operator runbook.
4. **Reconcile app composition.** Ensure the configured persistence mode is the actual source for memory, audit, executions, approvals, and task idempotency. Test clean startup for JSON, SQLite, and PostgreSQL.
5. **Keep gateway execution fixed and read-only.** Do not allow arbitrary model-selected shell, SQL, network, or filesystem execution.
6. **Keep root transition and external anchor work separate.** Require monotonic versioning, signature validation, crash recovery, and rollback tests.
7. **Keep S3/Terraform code-only.** No cloud apply, hosted Supabase mutation, or resource creation.
8. **Run clean-checkout acceptance** for each release slice: `npm ci`, `npm test`, `npm run check:syntax`, owner bootstrap, login/password rotation, harmless read-only task, refresh/state persistence, and logout denial.
9. **Record device acceptance honestly** for desktop, phone, and tablet. Do not infer Android or mobile browser acceptance from desktop Chromium.
10. **Require exact-SHA green CI** before considering a slice review-ready. No merge/release/deployment without separate owner authorization.

## Release boundaries

- No public deployment until HTTPS, durable sessions, operational controls, and security review are proven.
- No async worker activation until issue #189 and public task lifecycle issue #185 are complete.
- No cloud mutation or infrastructure apply.
- Close this issue only when every selected slice has a focused PR, documented dependencies, exact-SHA CI evidence, and a proven first-user workflow.

---

### Mainline evidence
- Current `main`: `f0fc76a6c831f0b656e2481f268927d3f5c3c422`.

- PR #336 and #325 are also based on the older mainline and require focused rebase/port plus exact-head verification; do not merge their stale heads directly.

It removes the current hard-coded test credential, allowlists only five exact historical test-fixture fingerprints, and runs a full-history Gitleaks scan on every PR/scheduled event. Exact PR head `0e3fc5aab2503b06618cb162fb8b3f4a53eaaae0` passed Gitleaks 8.24.3 across 3,986 commits with zero findings; all exact-head checks are green. No merge has been performed.

### User-value and commercial gate
Do not expand infrastructure or add platform features merely to increase engineering completeness. Before selecting another large build slice, validate the initial buyer problem: software teams building AI agents need controlled execution identity, approval, auditability, and safe recovery. Record customer evidence (interviews, a real workflow, measurable risk/cost reduction, and a pilot commitment) before treating this positioning or pricing as validated. No customer willingness-to-pay evidence is recorded here yet.

### Release / safety boundary
- Issue #225 remains open for actual phone, tablet, and desktop browser acceptance; Chromium CI is not device acceptance.
- Issue #189 remains open. Production asynchronous workers stay disabled until provider-aware idempotency and lifecycle gates pass.
- No public deployment, cloud apply, production data mutation, or merge is authorized by this status refresh.


---

items.title: Create fiducia-desktop.rs and fiducia-flutter with shared deep links
items.body:
## Objective

Create the required first-class desktop pair:

- `fiducia-cloud/fiducia-desktop.rs`
- `fiducia-cloud/fiducia-flutter`

Both targets are planned and must not be described as live until their remotes, builds, packages, tests, and supported-platform matrices are verified.

## Rust strategy

Use **GPUI** as a fully native Rust UI. Embedded WebViews are prohibited.

Rust owns lock/lease/consensus/cron state, validation, authentication, persistence, networking, telemetry aggregation, deep-link parsing, and privileged operations. GPUI owns dense virtualized views, timelines, keyboard navigation, custom rendering, and native windowing.

## Parallel delivery contract

- [ ] The Rust README names `fiducia-flutter`, links `docs/DESKTOP_TOOLKIT.md`, and states that Rust and Flutter feature development proceeds in parallel unless explicitly exempted.
- [ ] Rust `AGENTS.md` and the PR template require inspection of the Flutter companion and a no-change rationale for one-sided work.
- [ ] Flutter README/agent/PR guidance reciprocally names the Rust companion.
- [ ] Shared acceptance criteria, schemas, routes, telemetry/simulation fixtures, and conformance tests are versioned deliberately.
- [ ] Rust and Flutter platform/release status is reported separately.

## Deep links

Canonical family:

```text
https://<verified-fiducia-owned-host>/open/<route>?<bounded-query>
```

Fallback:

```text
fiducia://<route>?<bounded-query>
```

- [ ] Define shared route types and golden fixtures in the Fiducia interfaces package.
- [ ] Support cold start and delivery to an already-running/single-instance app.
- [ ] Support safe authentication resume and browser fallback.
- [ ] Validate exact host, route/version, tenant, node/group/resource identifiers, action, and bounded query values.
- [ ] Reject replay, expiry, unsafe returns, and unauthorized tenant/resource access.
- [ ] Require confirmation before privileged lock, lease, schedule, membership, or failover actions.
- [ ] Test macOS, Windows, Linux, Android, and iOS link behavior.

Passwords, bearer/service tokens, tenant secrets, private keys, and sensitive lock payloads are prohibited in URLs. Privileged handoffs use short-lived, single-use, audience-bound codes.

## Repository bootstrap

items.title: security review: hostile intake, tenancy, residency and data lifecycle
items.body:
Parent: #1. Cross-repo epic: tesserix/australis#20.

Review `docs/security/THREAT-MODEL.md` and ADR-0003.

## Required review scope

- Hostile PDF/image parser isolation, malware handling, MIME sniffing, decompression/pixel/page/time limits.
- IDOR prevention at upload, job, page, result, cache, review, event and deletion boundaries.
- SSRF prevention by refusing arbitrary URLs.
- Workload identity, least privilege, KMS/encryption, one-time PDF-password tokens and secret redaction.
- Provider retention and region-policy enforcement.
- Prompt injection: OCR content remains untrusted and cannot alter principal, tenant, directives, tools, schemas, callbacks or credentials.
- Webhook forgery/replay, duplicate delivery and confused-deputy scenarios.
- Audit, retention, erasure, backup-expiry truth, telemetry redaction and golden-corpus governance.
- Pinned supply chain, SBOM/provenance and least-privilege CI.

## Approval checklist

- [ ] Security owner approves threat model and negative-test plan
- [ ] Privacy/data owner approves data classes and lifecycle
- [ ] Platform owner approves sandbox/identity/network controls
- [ ] Prompt-injection containment is tested structurally, not only by prompt wording
- [ ] No raw content, secret, signed URL or sensitive filename may enter logs/traces/errors
- [ ] Production readiness includes restore and deletion verification

items.title: Claim review: ZPA, part 1 of 2 (127 claims)

labels.name: claim-review
labels.description: Claims the audit flagged, for a person (or a reviewing model) to decide

items.body:
Each claim below was flagged by the claim audit: a part of its statement, in **bold** where it can be marked, that its judges did not find any quote stating. Borderline claims (unmarked) had only low-confidence flags, about half of them real; *(overreach)* claims had a confident one. Each link opens the claim in its subject file, with its `evidence` quotes and any `conditions` just below; the rule is [the audit rubric](https://github.com/dvmrry/zscaler-skill/blob/ba606fe51cb698476b059b73cabddc3b6705c667/references/_meta/evals/claim-audit/rubric.md): every material part of the statement must be stated by a quote (an absence may rest on the search its conditions record). Tick a claim that is fine as written. Comment with the claim ID and what to change for one to narrow or to quote; it gets fixed in a pull request. Links are at commit ba606fe5. These claims were flagged in two independent full audit runs (2026-11-03); claims flagged in only one run are left out as likely noise.

- [ ] [`zpa.api.app-connectors-wire:version-profile-gid-key`](https://github.com/dvmrry/zscaler-skill/blob/ba606fe51cb698476b059b73cabddc3b6705c667/references/zpa/zpa.api.app-connectors-wire.json#L305) Inside a version profile's `versions` entries the Go SDK tags the profile reference `version_profile_gid`, in snake case, while its sibling `restartAfterUptimeInDays` is camel case. The Python ComponentLevelVersion model (which the AppConnectorController and App Connector group models build from their `version` key) looks up and emits the same `version_profile_gid` key, but **the Python client camel-cases every response key before a model reads it**.
- [ ] [`zpa.api.app-segments-wire:application-type-validation`](https://github.com/dvmrry/zscaler-skill/blob/ba606fe51cb698476b059b73cabddc3b6705c667/references/zpa/zpa.api.app-segments-wire.json#L816) The Go `GetByApplicationType` and `DeleteByApplicationType` reject any application type other than BROWSER_ACCESS, INSPECT or SECURE_REMOTE_ACCESS before sending a request, while the Python `get_segments_by_type` only requires a non-empty type and **`delete_segments_by_type` does not check it**; the API documents `applicationType` as a required string **without an enum**.
- [ ] [`zpa.api.app-segments-wire:delete-by-type-request`](https://github.com/dvmrry/zscaler-skill/blob/ba606fe51cb698476b059b73cabddc3b6705c667/references/zpa/zpa.api.app-segments-wire.json#L762) **Deleting a sub-application by type** is `DELETE /application/{id}/deleteAppByType` with the application type as a query parameter; the Go function sends only the type and the Microtenant filter, while Go's application segment, browser access, inspection and PRA deletes pass `ForceDelete: true`, and the Python function sends `applicationType` and an optional `microtenantId`.
- [ ] [`zpa.api.app-segments-wire:subapp-read-write-fields`](https://github.com/dvmrry/zscaler-skill/blob/ba606fe51cb698476b059b73cabddc3b6705c667/references/zpa/zpa.api.app-segments-wire.json#L206) The Go Inspection and PRA segment models **read their sub-applications from `inspectionApps` and `praApps` respectively**, and **write them through `commonAppsDto.appsConfig`**; the API create body defines `appsConfig` entries as CommonAppConfigDto.

- [ ] [`zpa.microtenants.share-and-move:python-move`](https://github.com/dvmrry/zscaler-skill/blob/ba606fe51cb698476b059b73cabddc3b6705c667/references/zpa/zpa.microtenants.share-and-move.json#L244) The Python SDK's `app_segment_move` **posts to `/application/{id}/move`** with `targetSegmentGroupId`, `targetMicrotenantId` and `targetServerGroupId` in the body and the source scope as the `microtenantId` query parameter.
- [ ] [`zpa.microtenants.share-and-move:python-share`](https://github.com/dvmrry/zscaler-skill/blob/ba606fe51cb698476b059b73cabddc3b6705c667/references/zpa/zpa.microtenants.share-and-move.json#L272) The Python SDK's `app_segment_share` **puts `shareToMicrotenants` to `/application/{id}/share`**, and its docstring says to send the attribute as an empty list to remove the share.
- [ ] [`zpa.policy.access-rule-order:go-reorder-calls`](https://github.com/dvmrry/zscaler-skill/blob/ba606fe51cb698476b059b73cabddc3b6705c667/references/zpa/zpa.policy.access-rule-order.json#L186) **The Go SDK has two reorder calls**: `Reorder`, which moves one rule with a PUT to `.../rule/{ruleId}/reorder/{newOrder}`, and `BulkReorder`, which takes a map of rule ID to order and PUTs to the policy set's `reorder` endpoint.
- [ ] [`zpa.policy.conditions:chrome-operand-forms`](https://github.com/dvmrry/zscaler-skill/blob/ba606fe51cb698476b059b73cabddc3b6705c667/references/zpa/zpa.policy.conditions.json#L268) *(overreach)* The Terraform provider requires CHROME_POSTURE_PROFILE operands to **carry a profile ID in values**, and CHROME_ENTERPRISE operands to carry entry_values with lhs managed and rhs true or false.
- [ ] [`zpa.policy.conditions:condition-block-single-type`](https://github.com/dvmrry/zscaler-skill/blob/ba606fe51cb698476b059b73cabddc3b6705c667/references/zpa/zpa.policy.conditions.json#L190) In the MCP server's **v2 access rule format** each condition block holds a single object type, multiple blocks are ANDed, and multiple operands or entry values inside one block are ORed.
- [ ] [`zpa.policy.evaluation-order:segment-then-rules`](https://github.com/dvmrry/zscaler-skill/blob/ba606fe51cb698476b059b73cabddc3b6705c667/references/zpa/zpa.policy.evaluation-order.json#L140) When a request arrives, Private Access **identifies the matching rule first**, choosing the rule that corresponds to the most specific application segment for the domain name or IP address if segments are part of the criteria.
- [ ] [`zpa.policy.multimatch:port-mismatch-dropped`](https://github.com/dvmrry/zscaler-skill/blob/ba606fe51cb698476b059b73cabddc3b6705c667/references/zpa/zpa.policy.multimatch.json#L144) When the more specific segment lacks the requested port, the access is dropped at the client level, traffic is not sent to the Private Access cloud, and the attempt is not visible in the diagnostics.
- [ ] [`zpa.policy.rule-fields:isolation-profile-required-for-isolate`](https://github.com/dvmrry/zscaler-skill/blob/ba606fe51cb698476b059b73cabddc3b6705c667/references/zpa/zpa.policy.rule-fields.json#L192) *(overreach)* The Python `add_isolation_rule` requires `zpn_isolation_profile_id` when the action is isolate and **checks nothing about the profile ID for other actions**.
- [ ] [`zpa.policy.rule-fields:reauth-force-new-v1`](https://github.com/dvmrry/zscaler-skill/blob/ba606fe51cb698476b059b73cabddc3b6705c667/references/zpa/zpa.policy.rule-fields.json#L87) **In the shared policy schema of the Terraform provider, used by the forwarding, access, timeout and redirection rule resources**, `reauth_timeout` and `reauth_idle_timeout` are ForceNew, so changing either on an existing rule plans a destroy and recreate.
- [ ] [`zpa.posture-profiles.policy-operand:lhs-is-udid`](https://github.com/dvmrry/zscaler-skill/blob/ba606fe51cb698476b059b73cabddc3b6705c667/references/zpa/zpa.posture-profiles.policy-operand.json#L117) **A POSTURE operand's lhs is the profile's posture_udid**, not its resource id: the data source note says to export posture_udid instead of the id, and **the access rule documentation says lhs is the posture_udid**.
- [ ] [`zpa.posture-profiles.policy-operand:v1-lookup`](https://github.com/dvmrry/zscaler-skill/blob/ba606fe51cb698476b059b73cabddc3b6705c667/references/zpa/zpa.posture-profiles.policy-operand.json#L182) **For v1 policy rule resources** the provider looks the POSTURE lhs up with GetByPostureUDID, so **a value that is not a known posture UDID fails the create or update**, and it requires rhs to be "true" or "false".
- [ ] [`zpa.posture-profiles.policy-operand:v2-no-lookup`](https://github.com/dvmrry/zscaler-skill/blob/ba606fe51cb698476b059b73cabddc3b6705c667/references/zpa/zpa.posture-profiles.policy-operand.json#L224) *(overreach)* For v2 policy rule resources the provider requires a non-empty lhs and an rhs of "true" or "false" for a POSTURE operand and **does not look the lhs up**.
- [ ] [`zpa.pra.app-segments:tf-app-types-forced`](https://github.com/dvmrry/zscaler-skill/blob/ba606fe51cb698476b059b73cabddc3b6705c667/references/zpa/zpa.pra.app-segments.json#L143) The Terraform PRA segment resource sets app_types to SECURE_REMOTE_ACCESS **on each existing PRA app it keeps when it updates a segment**, and on every PRA app it reads back into state.
- [ ] [`zpa.pra.credentials:credential-types`](https://github.com/dvmrry/zscaler-skill/blob/ba606fe51cb698476b059b73cabddc3b6705c667/references/zpa/zpa.pra.credentials.json#L90) Privileged credentials **come in three types**: Username+Password for RDP with an optional domain, SSH Key with a username, private key and optional passphrase, and Password for VNC or RealVNC.
- [ ] [`zpa.pra.credentials:type-immutable`](https://github.com/dvmrry/zscaler-skill/blob/ba606fe51cb698476b059b73cabddc3b6705c667/references/zpa/zpa.pra.credentials.json#L143) A credential's type cannot be changed after it is created and saved, **so a credential made for RDP cannot be reused for SSH**.
- [ ] [`zpa.pra.privileged-desktops:two-steps`](https://github.com/dvmrry/zscaler-skill/blob/ba606fe51cb698476b059b73cabddc3b6705c667/references/zpa/zpa.pra.privileged-desktops.json#L83) *(overreach)* **The repository has two CloudFormation templates**: permissions_policy_step_1.yml creates a customer-managed IAM policy and create_iam_role_and_trust_step_2.yml creates a cross-account role with a trust policy.
- [ ] [`zpa.pra.tooling:ansible-approval-lookup-ignores-windows`](https://github.com/dvmrry/zscaler-skill/blob/ba606fe51cb698476b059b73cabddc3b6705c667/references/zpa/zpa.pra.tooling.json#L226) The Ansible approval lookup compares the sorted email set and, when application IDs are supplied, the sorted application ID set, and **does not compare the approval's start or end window**.
- [ ] [`zpa.pra.tooling:working-hours-optional`](https://github.com/dvmrry/zscaler-skill/blob/ba606fe51cb698476b059b73cabddc3b6705c667/references/zpa/zpa.pra.tooling.json#L160) In the Python SDK pra_approval, working_hours is optional: **time conversion defaults to UTC when it is omitted**, and workingHours is sent only when the caller supplies it, because the API rejects a partial or empty workingHours object. The 1.9.34 release note records a working_hours fix.
- [ ] [`zpa.private-service-edges.api-surface:schedule-endpoints`](https://github.com/dvmrry/zscaler-skill/blob/ba606fe51cb698476b059b73cabddc3b6705c667/references/zpa/zpa.private-service-edges.api-surface.json#L220) The auto-delete schedule is read with GET /serviceEdgeSchedule, **which returns one schedule object rather than a list**, created with POST /serviceEdgeSchedule and updated with PUT /serviceEdgeSchedule/{id}; the body carries frequency, frequencyInterval, deleteDisabled and enabled, and **an optional microtenantId query parameter applies**.
- [ ] [`zpa.private-service-edges.client-selection:grace-distance`](https://github.com/dvmrry/zscaler-skill/blob/ba606fe51cb698476b059b73cabddc3b6705c667/references/zpa/zpa.private-service-edges.client-selection.json#L217) *(overreach)* Grace distance (**console: Public Service Edge Proximity Override**) allows a Private Service Edge group within a specified distance of the user to be prioritized over a closer Public Service Edge for Private Access.
